questions.explanation: We see the Sun, sunrise and rainbows in the day. Stars are in the sky all the time, but we can only see them at night.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: The Sun rises in the ___ and sets in the west.
questions.explanation: Every morning the Sun comes up in the east. In the evening it goes down in the west.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: The Earth ___, so we have day and night.
questions.explanation: The Earth spins round. The side facing the Sun has day and the side facing away has night.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: The Moon makes its own light.
questions.explanation: The Moon does not make light. It shines because it reflects light from the Sun.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: Shadows are shortest at midday.
questions.explanation: At midday the Sun is highest in the sky, so shadows are short.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: Put these in order, from morning to night.
sequence: The Sun rises in the east.
The Sun is high at midday.
The Sun sets in the west.
Stars come out at night.
questions.explanation: The Sun seems to climb up in the morning, is highest at midday and goes down in the evening. Then we see the stars.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: Mina shines a torch on a ball in a dark room. The torch stands for the…
questions.explanation: The torch is the Sun and the ball is the Earth. The lit side of the ball has day and the dark side has night.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.subskill: Sun and Moon in our culture
questions.stem: Match each one to what it means.
questions.explanation: The Sun and Moon matter to many people. Muslims break their fast at sunset in Ramadan. Eid begins when the new Moon is seen. Pohela Boishakh welcomes the new Bangla year.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: What is true about the Sun? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: The Sun rises in the east, is highest at midday and sets in the west. It does not go out at night. The Earth spins so our side faces away from it.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: Match each picture to what it shows.
questions.explanation: At sunrise the Sun comes up. At night we see stars. A full Moon looks round and bright. The Sun gives us light and heat.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: Raju wants to see the Sun. What is the safe way?
options: Look straight at it for a short time.
Look at the shadow it makes instead.
questions.explanation: Never look straight at the Sun. It can hurt your eyes. We can watch the shadows instead.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.subskill: Sun and Moon in our culture
questions.stem: On the last evening of Ramadan, Imran's family looks for the new Moon. Where should they look?
questions.explanation: A thin new Moon is low in the western sky just after sunset. When the family sees it, they know Eid will start the next day.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: At 12 o'clock Tuli plays outside. Her shadow is very short. Why?
options: The Sun is high in the sky.
questions.explanation: At midday the Sun is high in the sky, so shadows are short.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: Class 1 measured a stick's shadow. At 9 o'clock it was 6 hand spans. At 12 o'clock it was 1 hand span. At 3 o'clock it was 5 hand spans. The shadow was shortest at ___ o'clock.
questions.explanation: 1 hand span is the smallest number, so the shadow was shortest at 12 o'clock. The Sun is highest at midday.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: It is daytime for Nadia in Dhaka. Her uncle in another country says it is dark there. This can happen because the Earth spins.
questions.explanation: The Earth spins, so when one side faces the Sun, the other side faces away. It can be day in one country and night in another.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: Why do we have day and night?
questions.model_answer: The Earth spins. The side facing the Sun has day and the side facing away has night.
questions.explanation: The Sun does not really move. The Earth spins, so each side takes a turn facing the Sun.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: Look at the picture. The object blocks the ___, so there is a shadow.
questions.image_alt: A torch shines on an object and the object's shadow falls on a screen.
questions.explanation: A shadow forms behind an object when the object blocks the light from the torch or the Sun.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: Mina measured a shadow. 9 o'clock: 6 hand spans. 12 o'clock: 1 hand span. 3 o'clock: 5 hand spans. When was the Sun highest in the sky?
questions.explanation: The shortest shadow means the Sun is highest. The shadow was shortest at 12 o'clock.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: Look at the picture. In the morning the shadow points to the west. Where is the Sun in the morning?
questions.image_alt: A stick and its shadow in the morning, at midday and in the evening. The morning shadow points west and the evening shadow points east.
questions.explanation: A shadow falls on the opposite side to the Sun. The shadow points west, so the Sun is in the east. That is where the Sun rises.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: Rafi says: 'It is night because the Sun goes out.' Which idea is right?
options: The Earth spins, so our side turns away from the Sun.
The Sun goes to sleep at night.
questions.explanation: The Sun does not go out. The Earth spins, so at night our side faces away from the Sun.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: Match each kind of weather to what you wear or use.
questions.explanation: An umbrella keeps us dry in the rain. A sun hat keeps the Sun off our head. A scarf and jumper keep us warm on a cold day.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: Look at the weather tools. Which letter is the rain gauge?
questions.image_alt: Five weather tools lettered A to E: a thermometer, a rain gauge, a wind vane, an anemometer and a barometer.
questions.explanation: B is the rain gauge. It collects rain so we can see how much fell. A is the thermometer, which shows how hot it is.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: Which picture shows windy weather?
questions.explanation: The wind picture shows air moving. Windy weather moves leaves, flags and kites.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: Which weather tool would you use? Sort each job.
items: how full the rain bottle is
questions.explanation: A thermometer measures how hot or cold. A rain gauge collects rain. A wind flag points the way the wind blows.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: The monsoon brings good things and problems. Sort them.
questions.explanation: Monsoon rain gives rice fields water and turns the land green. Too much rain can make the rivers overflow and cause floods.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: We measure how hot it is with a ___. We measure rain with a rain ___.
questions.explanation: A thermometer measures how hot or cold it is. A rain gauge measures how much rain falls.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: The weather is the same every day.
questions.explanation: The weather changes from day to day. One day can be sunny and the next day can be rainy.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: A weather forecast tells us what the weather will be like.
questions.explanation: Forecasters use patterns in the weather to say what tomorrow will be like.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: In Bangladesh, the wet rainy season is called the…
questions.explanation: The wet season is the monsoon. It brings heavy rain, and rivers fill up.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: The seasons come round every year. Start with hot summer. What comes next?
sequence: hot summer
the rainy season (monsoon)
cool winter
questions.explanation: In Bangladesh the weather follows a pattern: hot summer, then the wet rainy season, then cool winter. Then the pattern starts again.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: Which pictures show wet weather? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Rain clouds, storm clouds and an umbrella in the rain all show wet weather. The Sun and the wind are dry.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: Match each weather word to its meaning.
pairs: what the air outside is like
a time of year with its own weather
telling what the weather will be
questions.explanation: Weather is what the air outside is like each day. A season is a time of year with its own weather. A forecast says what the weather will be.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: Class 1 looked at the sky for 10 days. Sunny: 5 days. Cloudy: 3 days. Rainy: 2 days. The most common weather was ___.
questions.explanation: Sunny has the biggest number, 5 days. So sunny was the most common weather.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: Look at the water cycle. Which number shows rain falling?
questions.image_alt: The water cycle with five stages numbered 1 to 5. Number 3 shows rain falling from a cloud.
questions.explanation: Number 3 is rain falling from the cloud. Rain gives us water for rivers, ponds and rice fields.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: Water goes round and round. Put the journey of the water in order.
sequence: The Sun warms the river water.
The water rises into the air.
The water makes clouds.
Rain falls from the clouds.
Rain runs into the rivers.
questions.explanation: The Sun warms water so it rises into the air and makes clouds. The rain falls and runs back into the rivers. Then the journey starts again.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: Raju is flying his kite. Dark clouds come and thunder rumbles. What should he do?
questions.explanation: In a storm we go indoors. A kite or a tall tree can be dangerous in thunder and lightning.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: Mina plays outside on a hot sunny day. What should she do? Choose all that are right.
options: Stay in the Sun all day.
questions.explanation: A hat, water and shade keep us cool on a hot day. A thick jumper makes us hotter, and staying in the Sun all day is not safe.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: Why do farmers like the monsoon rain?
options: It makes the soil very dry.
It stops the rice seeds growing.
questions.explanation: Rice grows best in fields full of water. The monsoon rain fills the fields so farmers can plant rice.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: The radio says heavy rain is coming and the river may flood. What should Sumi's family do?
options: Go to play in the river water.
Stay outside and ignore the news.
Move to a higher, safe place.
questions.explanation: A forecast helps us get ready. Moving to a higher, safe place keeps the family away from the flood water.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: Tuli empties her rain gauge every evening. Today it holds more water than yesterday. This means more rain fell today.
questions.explanation: A rain gauge collects the rain that falls. More water in the gauge means more rain fell.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: Look at the weather tools. Which letter shows which way the wind blows?
questions.image_alt: Five weather tools lettered A to E: a thermometer, a rain gauge, a wind vane that points the way the wind blows, an anemometer and a barometer.
questions.explanation: C is the wind vane. It turns and points the way the wind is blowing, like a wind flag.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: Class 1 looked at the sky for 10 days. Sunny: 5 days. Cloudy: 3 days. Rainy: 2 days. On how many days was it cloudy or rainy?
questions.explanation: 3 cloudy days plus 2 rainy days is 5 days.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: Class 1 saw sunny weather on 5 of 10 days. Raju says: 'It will be sunny tomorrow for sure.' Is Raju right?
questions.explanation: Patterns help us guess, but the weather can change. Tomorrow could be cloudy or rainy. A forecast is a good guess, not a sure thing.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: Why do people listen to the weather forecast in the monsoon?
questions.model_answer: To know when heavy rain and floods may come, so they can stay safe.
questions.explanation: Too much rain can bring floods. The forecast tells people to get ready and stay safe.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: Which picture shows something that harms the environment?
questions.explanation: Smoke makes the air dirty, so it harms the environment. Bins, trees and cloth bags help to keep it clean.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: Which bin? Match each piece of waste to its bin.
questions.explanation: We sort waste by what it is made of. Paper, plastic and metal can be recycled. A mango peel is food waste, so it goes to compost.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: Which pictures show a healthy environment? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Trees, clean water and litter in a bin all help keep the environment healthy. Oil in water and smoke harm it.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: Does it help or harm the environment? Sort the pictures.
questions.explanation: Trees clean the air. A cloth bag can be used again and again, and a bin keeps litter off the ground. Oil and smoke make the water and air dirty.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: Which picture shows reusing?
questions.explanation: We can use a cloth bag again and again. Reuse means to use something again.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: This banana skin is food waste. Where should it go?
questions.image_alt: A banana.
questions.explanation: Food waste rots and makes the soil rich. We put it in compost, not in the paper, metal or plastic bins.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: Reduce, reuse or recycle? Sort each idea.
items: use both sides of the paper
take only the food you can eat
use an old jar as a pencil pot
carry a cloth bag again and again
put cans in the metal bin
put old paper in the paper bin
questions.explanation: Reduce means use less. Reuse means use again. Recycle means make something new from old things.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: The three Rs are reduce, reuse and ___.
questions.explanation: Reduce, reuse and recycle are the three Rs. They help us make less rubbish.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: Food waste can be made into compost.
questions.explanation: Food waste rots and makes the soil rich. Gardeners use compost to help plants grow.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: Cutting down lots of trees helps keep our air clean.
questions.explanation: Trees help keep the air clean and are homes for animals. Cutting down lots of trees harms the environment.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: What does a healthy environment have? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: A healthy environment has clean water, plenty of trees and fresh air. Litter and smoke make it unhealthy.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to sort the class rubbish.
sequence: Put on gloves.
Empty the bin onto a sheet.
Sort the waste into groups.
Count each group.
Wash your hands.
questions.explanation: We wear gloves first to stay safe. Then we empty, sort and count the waste, and wash our hands at the end.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: Reduce means to use less.
questions.explanation: To reduce is to use less. When we use less, we make less rubbish.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: Class 1 sorted their bin. Paper: 12. Plastic: 8. Food: 5. Metal: 2. They had the most ___ waste.
questions.explanation: 12 is the biggest number, so there was most paper waste. They can use both sides of the paper to make less.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: Match each harmful action to the problem it causes.
questions.explanation: Litter can hurt animals, and smoke makes the air dirty. Dirty water can make people ill. Trees are homes for animals.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: Moung sees a broken glass bottle on the playground. What should he do?
options: Pick it up with his hands.
questions.explanation: Broken glass can cut us. We never touch it. We tell a teacher so a grown-up can clear it safely.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: Plastic bags blow around Tuli's playground. What is a good plan?
options: Put labelled bins in each class.
Burn all the bags behind the school.
Throw the bags into the pond.
questions.explanation: Bins in every class help children put litter in the right place. Burning bags makes smoke, and bags in a pond harm the water and animals.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: After cooking, Anika's family has fruit peels and vegetable scraps. What can they do?
questions.explanation: Peels and scraps rot and make rich compost for plants. Burning and throwing them in the river harm the air and the water.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: At the market, Nadia takes her own cloth bag instead of a new plastic bag each time. This helps the environment.
questions.explanation: Using a cloth bag again and again means less plastic is thrown away. This is reusing.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: How can our school stay clean and healthy? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Bins, trees and clean toilets keep a school healthy. Litter makes the playground dirty, and running taps waste water.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: Write one thing you can do to keep your school clean.
questions.model_answer: I can put my litter in the bin.
questions.explanation: Putting litter in the bin, sorting waste and planting trees all help keep a school clean and healthy.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: Class 1 sorted their bin. Paper: 12. Plastic: 8. Food: 5. Metal: 2. How many pieces of waste were there in all?
questions.explanation: 12 + 8 = 20. 20 + 5 = 25. 25 + 2 = 27. There were 27 pieces of waste.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: Class 1 had 12 pieces of paper, 8 of plastic, 5 of food and 2 of metal. They want to make less rubbish. What is the best first plan?
options: Use both sides of the paper.
Use fewer metal tins in class.
questions.explanation: Paper was the biggest pile. Using both sides of the paper makes the biggest change.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: Class 1 found 12 pieces of paper, 5 of food and 2 of metal. Food and metal together are how many fewer than paper?
questions.explanation: Food and metal together are 5 + 2 = 7. Paper is 12. 12 take away 7 is 5, so food and metal together are 5 fewer.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Which picture shows a natural material?
questions.explanation: Wood comes from trees, so it is natural. Plastic and glass are made by people.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Natural or made by people? Sort the pictures.
questions.explanation: Wood, stone and wool come from nature. Plastic, glass and paper are made by people.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Wool is a natural material.
questions.explanation: Wool comes from sheep, so it is natural.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Paper is found in nature. People do not make it.
questions.explanation: People make paper in factories or by hand. It is not found in nature.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: We can ___ a sponge by pressing it hard.
questions.explanation: Pressing hard on a sponge squashes it.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Match each action to the thing you do it to.
questions.explanation: We squash a sponge, stretch a rubber band, twist a wet towel and bend a pipe cleaner.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Which one can we stretch?
questions.explanation: A balloon stretches when we blow it up. A stone and a brick do not stretch.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Which goes back to its shape after squashing?
questions.explanation: A sponge goes back to its shape. Clay stays in its new shape.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Why is a ball made of rubber, not stone?
questions.model_answer: Rubber bounces and is soft. A stone is hard and would hurt.
questions.explanation: Rubber is soft and bounces. A stone is hard and does not bounce.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to make a clay pot.
sequence: Dig clay from the river bank.
Squash and shape the clay on the wheel.
Dry the pot in the sun.
Heat the pot in a hot kiln.
questions.explanation: Mr Paul digs the clay, shapes it on the wheel, dries the pot and then heats it in the kiln.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Mr Paul heats clay pots in a kiln. What happens?
questions.explanation: Heating in the kiln makes the clay hard. It will never go soft again.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Joy wants a toy he can squash and shape. Which is best?
questions.explanation: Clay is soft and can be squashed into new shapes. Stone and glass are hard.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Nadia twists a wet towel to dry it. This changes its shape.
questions.explanation: Twisting changes the shape of a towel and squeezes the water out.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Which are made by people? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Plastic, glass and paper are made by people. Stone and wool come from nature.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Match each picture to its material.
questions.explanation: A chair is made of wood, a key of metal and a bottle of plastic. Socks are made of cloth.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Which picture shows something made of metal?
questions.explanation: A key is made of metal. A newspaper is paper and a teddy bear is cloth.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: A sponge stays flat after you squash it and let go.
questions.explanation: A sponge goes back to its shape. Clay is the one that stays flat.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Squashing, bending, twisting and ___ change the shape of materials.
questions.explanation: The four ways to change shape are squashing, bending, twisting and stretching.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Class 1 test: thin band 14 cm, medium 11 cm, thick 8 cm. Which stretched most?
questions.explanation: The thin band became the longest, 14 cm, so it stretched the most.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Thin band: 14 cm. Thick band: 8 cm. How much longer is the thin band?
questions.explanation: 14 minus 8 is 6, so the thin band was 6 cm longer.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Rafi squashes clay and a sponge, then lets go. What happens?

options.text: The clay stays flat. The sponge springs back.
Both go back to their shape.

questions.explanation: Clay stays squashed. A sponge goes back to its shape.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Sort by what happens after you squash or stretch.
questions.explanation: A sponge and a rubber band go back to their shape. Clay, play dough and a bent pipe cleaner stay in the new shape.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Jute is a natural material.
questions.explanation: Jute comes from plants, so it is a natural material.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Which picture shows something made by people?
questions.explanation: A plastic bottle is made by people in a factory. Wood and stone come from nature.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Is it heating or cooling? Sort the changes.
questions.explanation: Ice melts, an egg cooks and water boils when they are heated. Water freezes, jelly sets and melted chocolate goes hard when they are cooled.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: An ice cube sits in the hot sun. What will it become?
questions.image_alt: An ice cube.
questions.explanation: Heat melts ice into water.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Which picture shows something that melts in the sun?
questions.explanation: Ice cream melts when it gets warm. A rock and a coin do not melt in the sun.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Which can melt when heated? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Ice, chocolate and ice cream melt when they are heated. A brick and a key do not melt in everyday heat.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Water boils and turns to steam.
questions.explanation: When water is heated until it boils, it turns into steam.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: This egg is cooked. It can turn back into a raw egg.
questions.image_alt: A fried egg in a pan.
questions.explanation: A cooked egg cannot go back. Cooking is a change that cannot go back.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Water turns into ice when it is ___.
questions.explanation: Cooling water makes it freeze into ice.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Salt ___ in water and seems to disappear.
questions.explanation: Salt dissolves in water. It mixes in and seems to disappear.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
questions.explanation: Melt is solid to liquid. Freeze is liquid to solid. Dissolve is mixing into water and seeming to disappear. Boil is water turning to steam.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to make pitha.
sequence: Mix rice flour and water into dough.
Steam the pitha over hot water.
The dough turns into a firm cake.
Share the warm pitha.
questions.explanation: Grandma mixes flour and water into dough. She steams it over hot water. The dough turns into a firm cake.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Mina leaves butter in the hot sun. What happens?
questions.explanation: Heat melts butter.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Rina wants ice cubes for a drink. Where should she put water?
questions.explanation: Cooling water makes it freeze. A freezer is very cold.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Imran stirs sugar in his tea. What happens to the sugar?
questions.explanation: Sugar dissolves in hot tea. It mixes in and seems to disappear.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Only grown-ups use the stove and hot water.
questions.explanation: Stoves and hot water can burn us. Children ask a grown-up for help.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Joy puts melted chocolate in the fridge. It goes hard again.
questions.explanation: Cooling makes melted chocolate go hard again. This change can go back.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Steam rises from a hot drink. When steam cools, it turns into...
questions.image_alt: A hot drink with steam.
questions.explanation: Steam turns back into water drops when it cools.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Match each picture to what happens.
questions.explanation: Ice melts when heated. A fried egg cooks and goes hard. Water drops freeze into ice when cooled.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Why does ice cream melt on a hot day?
questions.model_answer: The hot day heats the ice cream, so it melts into a liquid.
questions.explanation: Heat from the air and sun warms the ice cream. A solid ice cream turns into a liquid.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Which things dissolve in water? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Salt and sugar dissolve in water. Sand, rice and coins do not.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Can the change go back? Sort the changes.
questions.explanation: Ice melting, chocolate melting and water freezing can go back. A cooked egg and steamed pitha cannot.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Melting times: sun 10 minutes, classroom 25, fridge 60. Where did ice melt fastest?
questions.explanation: The shortest time was in the sun, 10 minutes, so ice melted fastest there.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Fridge: 60 minutes. Sun: 10 minutes. How many more minutes in the fridge?
questions.explanation: 60 minus 10 is 50, so the ice took 50 minutes longer in the fridge.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Is it a fair test to use ice cubes of different sizes?
questions.explanation: Big ice cubes take longer to melt. For a fair test the ice cubes must be the same size.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Sand dissolves in water.
questions.explanation: Sand does not dissolve. It sinks to the bottom.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Which are light sources? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: The Sun, a candle and a torch give out light. The Moon only reflects the Sun's light and a mirror reflects light.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Does it give out light? Sort the pictures.
questions.explanation: The Sun, a candle and a light bulb give out light. The Moon, a mirror and a book do not.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: The Moon is a light source.
questions.explanation: The Moon does not make light. It reflects light from the Sun.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: A shadow forms when light is blocked.
questions.explanation: When something blocks the light, a dark shadow forms behind it.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Sounds are made by vibrations.
questions.explanation: A vibration is a very fast shake. Every sound starts with one.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Darkness is when there is no ___.
questions.explanation: Darkness means there is no light, so we cannot see.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: To vibrate means to shake very ___.
questions.explanation: Vibrate means to shake very fast. A drum skin vibrates when you hit it.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Match each instrument to how we make its sound.
questions.explanation: We hit a drum, pluck the strings of a guitar and shake maracas. Each one vibrates to make sound.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Look at the picture. What blocks the light?
questions.image_alt: A torch, an object and its shadow on a screen.
questions.explanation: The object stops the light from the torch reaching the screen. The dark shape behind it is the shadow.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Which picture shows something that makes a sound?
questions.explanation: A bell makes a sound when it rings. A candle and a mirror do not make sound.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Which picture shows what we hear with?
questions.explanation: We hear sounds with our ears.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: The lights go out at night. What can Nadia use to see?
questions.explanation: A torch gives out light, so Nadia can see. A mirror and a radio do not make light.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Sumi holds a card between a lamp and the wall. What forms?
questions.explanation: The card blocks the light, so a dark shadow forms on the wall.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Imran plucks a rubber band. It makes a sound. Why?
questions.explanation: A plucked band shakes very fast. This vibration makes the sound.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Moung can see his toys in a completely dark room.
questions.explanation: We cannot see anything when there is no light.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Put the steps in order for a shadow puppet show.
sequence: Switch on the lamp.
Hold a puppet between the lamp and the cloth.
A dark shadow forms on the cloth.
questions.explanation: The lamp gives light. The puppet blocks the light. Then a dark shadow forms on the cloth.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Why does a drum make a sound when you hit it?
questions.model_answer: The drum skin vibrates (shakes very fast) when you hit it.
questions.explanation: Hitting the drum makes the drum skin shake very fast. This vibration makes the sound.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Toy far: shadow 8 cm. Middle: 14 cm. Near: 25 cm. What happens as it gets nearer?
questions.explanation: The shadow grows from 8 cm to 25 cm as the toy gets nearer the torch.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Near shadow: 25 cm. Far shadow: 8 cm. How much bigger is the near one?
questions.explanation: 25 minus 8 is 17, so the near shadow is 17 cm bigger.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Lina says the Moon is bright, so it makes light. Is she right?

options.text: Yes, the Moon is a big lamp.
Yes, it makes light like a star.

questions.explanation: The Moon only looks bright because it reflects light from the Sun. It is not a light source.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Which make sounds? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: A drum, a loudspeaker and a barking dog all make sounds. A rock and a candle do not.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: We need light to see things.
questions.explanation: Without light we cannot see anything.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: What is the biggest light source for Earth?
questions.explanation: The Sun is the biggest light source. It lights up the day.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: A shadow has the same shape as the thing blocking the light.
questions.explanation: A shadow has the shape of the object that blocks the light.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: The lamp in this circuit will light.
questions.image_alt: A circuit with a cell, a lamp and a closed switch.
questions.explanation: The loop is complete and the switch is closed, so electricity flows round and the lamp lights.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: Why is the lamp off in this circuit?
questions.image_alt: A circuit with a cell, a lamp and an open switch.
questions.explanation: The open switch makes a gap in the loop. Electricity cannot flow round, so the lamp stays off.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: Match each part of a circuit to its job.
questions.explanation: A cell pushes electricity round. A wire carries it. A switch turns the circuit on and off. A lamp gives light.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: Is it safe or not safe? Sort the actions.
items: asking an adult to plug in
touching a switch with wet hands
questions.explanation: We use torches with batteries and ask an adult to plug things in. We never touch switches with wet hands or poke sockets.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: Does it use electricity? Sort the pictures.
questions.explanation: A fan, a television and a mobile phone use electricity. A ball, a chair and a teddy bear do not.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: A circuit is a loop.
questions.explanation: A circuit is a complete loop. Electricity flows round it from the cell, through the lamp and back.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: Electricity from the wall is safe to touch.
questions.explanation: Electricity from the wall is dangerous. Never touch sockets or wires.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: A switch can make a gap in a circuit.
questions.explanation: Opening a switch makes a gap, so the circuit is off. Closing it fills the gap.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: A lamp lights when the circuit is ___.
questions.explanation: Electricity can only flow round a complete circuit with no gaps.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: A cell is a battery that stores ___.
questions.explanation: A cell stores electricity and pushes it round the circuit.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to make a lamp light.
sequence: Join the cell, wires and lamp in a loop.
Check there are no gaps.
Close the switch.
The lamp lights.
questions.explanation: Join the parts in a loop, check there are no gaps, close the switch and then the lamp lights.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: Which part turns a circuit on and off?
questions.explanation: A switch opens and closes the circuit. A lamp gives light and a wire carries electricity.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: Which picture shows where solar electricity comes from?
questions.explanation: A solar panel turns sunlight into electricity.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: Where does electricity come from? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Sunlight, wind and moving water can all make electricity. A stone and a teddy bear cannot.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: There are no wires on Shuvo's char. Where does his electricity come from?
questions.explanation: Shuvo's family has a solar panel on the roof. It turns sunlight into electricity.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: Anika's hands are wet. A switch is on the wall. What should she do?
questions.explanation: Wet hands and electricity are dangerous. Anika asks an adult for help.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: Mina's toy light does not work. A wire has fallen off the cell. Why?
questions.explanation: The wire is part of the loop. With a wire off, there is a gap and electricity cannot flow.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: At night, Shuvo's battery lights the lamps.
questions.explanation: The solar panel charges the battery in the day. At night the battery lights the lamps.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: Why is a solar panel useful on the char?
questions.model_answer: There are no electricity wires on the char, so the solar panel makes electricity from sunlight.
questions.explanation: There are no electricity wires on the char. A solar panel makes electricity from sunlight.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: What happens to the bulb in a complete loop?

sim.task: Open Circuit Construction Kit: DC. Drag a battery, a light bulb and wires onto the board. Join them in one complete loop with no gaps. Watch the bulb.

questions.explanation: A bulb lights only when the loop is complete. Electricity flows from the battery through the bulb and back.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: The bulb stays lit when the switch is open.

sim.task: Open Circuit Construction Kit: DC. Make a loop with a battery, a bulb and wires, and add a switch. Click the switch to open it, then click it again to close it. Watch the bulb each time.

questions.explanation: An open switch makes a gap in the loop, so the bulb goes out. Closing the switch lights it again.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: A wire is off the loop. You close the switch. Does the lamp light?

options.text: No, it still has a gap.

questions.explanation: The missing wire leaves a gap, so closing the switch does not help.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: Each torch uses 2 cells. How many cells do 3 torches need?
questions.explanation: 2 + 2 + 2 = 6, so 3 torches need 6 cells.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: Metal things such as a coin let electricity pass through.
questions.explanation: Metals let electricity through. Things like a rubber eraser do not.

questions.title: I Am a Scientist
questions.stem: What does it mean to **observe**?
options: to make a guess before a test
to look closely using your senses
questions.explanation: To observe is to look closely and use your senses (never taste in science). Guessing, recording and sharing are other science jobs.

questions.title: I Am a Scientist
questions.stem: Which tool measures how hot or cold something is?
questions.explanation: A thermometer measures temperature. A ruler measures length and a stopwatch measures time.

questions.title: I Am a Scientist
questions.stem: Match each tool to its job.
questions.explanation: Each tool measures one thing: a ruler for length, a thermometer for hot or cold, a stopwatch for time, scales for weight. A hand lens (magnifying glass) makes small things look bigger.

questions.title: I Am a Scientist
questions.stem: A ___ is what you think will happen before you test it.
questions.explanation: A prediction is what you think will happen. After the test you check whether your prediction came true.

questions.title: I Am a Scientist
questions.stem: In science, you can taste any new food or liquid to find out what it is like.
questions.explanation: Never taste or smell things in science unless your teacher says it is safe. Some things that look harmless can make you ill.

questions.title: I Am a Scientist
questions.stem: Which sense would you use to find out each thing?
items: if the school bell is ringing
if the sand is wet or dry
if the flower has a sweet smell
questions.explanation: We use our eyes to see colour, our ears to hear sounds, our skin to feel rough or smooth, and our nose to smell.

questions.title: I Am a Scientist
questions.stem: Put the steps of an investigation in the right order.
sequence: Ask a question.
Make a prediction.
Do a fair test.
Measure and record what happens.
Tell others what you found.
questions.explanation: Scientists ask a question first, then predict, test fairly, measure and record, and finally tell others what they found.

questions.title: I Am a Scientist
questions.stem: Which of these questions can we answer by doing an investigation? Choose all that are right.
options: Does a plant need water to grow?
Which paper towel soaks up the most water?
questions.explanation: We can test 'Which ball bounces highest?', 'Does a plant need water?' and 'Which paper towel soaks up most water?' by trying things out. 'Which flower is prettiest?' is an opinion, so it cannot be tested.

questions.title: I Am a Scientist
questions.stem: In a fair test, you change…
options: as many things as you like
questions.explanation: A fair test changes only one thing and keeps everything else the same. Then you know what caused any difference.

questions.title: I Am a Scientist
questions.stem: Sumi and Lina want to find out which ball bounces higher, a rubber ball or a cloth ball. Sumi drops hers from a chair and Lina drops hers from a table. How can they make it a fair test?
options: Drop both balls from the same height.
Drop each ball on a different floor.
Drop the rubber ball a little harder.
Let each child choose any height.
questions.explanation: The balls must be dropped from the same height, or the height could be the reason for the difference. Only the type of ball should change.

questions.title: I Am a Scientist
questions.stem: Tuli is helping at the market. She wants to find out how heavy a mango is. Which tool should she use?
questions.explanation: Scales (such as a balance) measure how heavy something is. A ruler measures length, a stopwatch measures time and a thermometer measures temperature.

questions.title: I Am a Scientist
questions.stem: Arif finds a small red berry on a plant in the school garden. He wonders what it tastes like. What is the safest thing to do?
options: Taste a tiny bit to check.
Ask a friend to taste it first.
Squash it and rub it on his skin.
Look closely, draw it and ask his teacher.
questions.explanation: Some berries are poisonous, so we never taste unknown things. We can look closely, draw, and ask the teacher.

questions.title: I Am a Scientist
questions.stem: Class 2 visits the village pond to observe tadpoles. Which are safe and scientific things to do? Choose all that are right.
options: look closely and draw what you see
stay back from the edge with your teacher
lean far over the water alone
questions.explanation: Looking closely, drawing, staying back from the edge and washing hands are all safe. Tasting pond water or leaning over the water alone is dangerous.

questions.title: I Am a Scientist
questions.stem: Look at the three thermometers. Which one shows the hottest temperature?
questions.image_alt: Three thermometers lettered A, B and C with the liquid at different heights.
questions.explanation: The liquid in a thermometer rises when it is hotter. In C the liquid is highest, at about 40 °C, so C is the hottest.

questions.title: I Am a Scientist
questions.stem: Mina wants to find out which bird is singing in the tree. Which part of her body helps her most?
questions.explanation: We hear with our ears. Eyes help us see the bird, but a song is a sound.

questions.title: I Am a Scientist
questions.stem: Look at each animal. Sort them by whether the animal has wings.
questions.explanation: We can sort living things by features we can see. Birds, butterflies and bees have wings. Fish, snakes, cats and frogs do not.

questions.title: I Am a Scientist
questions.stem: Rina and Sami race toy cars down a slope. Rina gives her car a push, but Sami just lets his car go. Why is this not a fair test?
questions.model_answer: Rina pushed her car but Sami did not, so more than one thing was different. Both cars should just be let go.
questions.explanation: A fair test changes only one thing. Here the push is a second change, so we cannot tell why one car won. Both cars should just be let go.

questions.title: I Am a Scientist
questions.stem: We use a ___ to measure how long something is and ___ to measure how heavy it is.
questions.explanation: A ruler measures length in centimetres. Scales measure how heavy something is.

questions.title: I Am a Scientist
questions.stem: Class 2B dropped balls from the same height (example data). The rubber ball bounced 70 cm and the plastic ball bounced 40 cm. The rubber ball bounced ___ cm higher.
questions.explanation: Subtract to compare: 70 − 40 = 30. The rubber ball bounced 30 cm higher.

questions.title: I Am a Scientist
questions.stem: Match each science word to its meaning.
pairs: say what you think will happen
find out how long, heavy or hot
write or draw what you found
questions.explanation: These key words describe what scientists do: observe, predict, measure, record and run a fair test.

questions.title: I Am a Scientist
questions.stem: A prediction can turn out to be wrong, and that is still useful to a scientist.
questions.explanation: A wrong prediction is not a failure. It tells us something new and helps us think again and ask better questions.

questions.title: I Am a Scientist
questions.stem: Rumi counted the ducks on the lake once a month (example data): November 10, December 25, January 40, February 20, March 5. Which sentence do her counts support best?
options: The number of ducks went up every month.
The number of ducks went up until January, then went down.
There were more ducks in March than in November.
The number of ducks stayed the same all winter.
questions.explanation: The numbers go up to 40 in January and then go down to 5 in March. We should only write what the counts really show.

questions.title: I Am a Scientist
questions.stem: Which plan is a fair test of which cloth dries fastest?
options: Two wet cloths of the same size, one cotton and one nylon, hung side by side in the sun.
Wet cotton cloth in the sun and wet nylon cloth in the shade.
A big wet cotton cloth and a small wet nylon cloth in the sun.
A wet cotton cloth in the sun and a dry nylon cloth in the sun.
questions.explanation: Only the type of cloth should change. Plan B uses the same size, the same wetness and the same place. The other plans change two things at once.

questions.title: I Am a Scientist
questions.stem: Raju's class tests which paper towel soaks up the most water, brand A or brand B. Name two things they must keep the same.
questions.model_answer: They must use the same amount of water and the same size of paper towel (and soak them for the same time).
questions.explanation: Everything except the brand must stay the same: the amount of water, the size of the towel and the time it soaks. Then any difference is caused by the brand.

questions.title: I Am a Scientist
questions.stem: Look at the thermometers. Imran says that B is 30 degrees hotter than A.
questions.image_alt: Three thermometers lettered A, B and C with the liquid at different heights.
questions.explanation: A reads 5 °C and B reads 25 °C. 25 − 5 = 20, so B is 20 degrees hotter, not 30.

questions.title: I Am a Scientist
questions.stem: The inside of a healthy body is about 37 °C. Which thermometer shows about that temperature?
questions.image_alt: Three thermometers lettered A, B and C with the liquid at different heights.
questions.explanation: 37 °C is a little less than 40 °C. Thermometer B is just below the 40 mark. A (about 12 °C) is far too cold and C (about 48 °C) is far too hot.

questions.title: Plants and Their Parts
questions.stem: Which part of a plant takes in water from the soil?
questions.explanation: Roots take in water from the soil and hold the plant in place. The stem then carries the water up.

questions.title: Plants and Their Parts
questions.stem: Look at the plant. Which number shows the part that takes in water from the soil?
questions.image_alt: A plant with five parts numbered 1 to 5.
questions.explanation: Part 4 is the roots. They grow under the ground, take in water and hold the plant in the soil.

questions.title: Plants and Their Parts
questions.stem: Look at the plant. Which number shows the part that holds and protects the seeds?
questions.image_alt: A plant with five parts numbered 1 to 5.
questions.explanation: Part 5 is the fruit. A fruit such as a mango holds and protects the seeds. The flower (1) makes the seeds.

questions.title: Plants and Their Parts
questions.stem: A white flower stands in coloured water. After one day the petals have the same colour. What does this show?
questions.image_alt: A white flower stem standing in a jar of coloured water, with the petals now coloured.
options: The petals make their own colour.
The flower drinks water through its petals.
Water goes down the stem to the roots.
Water travels up the stem to the petals.
questions.explanation: The coloured water travelled up the stem to the petals. The stem carries water from the roots up to the leaves and flowers.

questions.title: Plants and Their Parts
questions.stem: Look at the four plants. How does a plant look when it gets no light?
questions.image_alt: Four potted plants: one healthy and three that are missing water, light or warmth.
questions.explanation: Without light a plant turns pale and weak, because its leaves cannot make food. A plant with no water is the one that wilts and droops.

questions.title: Plants and Their Parts
questions.stem: Look at the four plants. What happened to the plant that was too cold?
questions.image_alt: Four potted plants: one healthy and three that are missing water, light or warmth.
questions.explanation: Plants need the right temperature. When it is too cold, a plant grows very little and stays small.

questions.title: Plants and Their Parts
questions.stem: Which part of a plant is each of these foods? Sort the pictures.
questions.explanation: A carrot is a root. Leafy greens and herbs are leaves. Mangoes, tomatoes and bananas are fruits, because they hold the seeds.

questions.title: Plants and Their Parts
questions.stem: Water goes into the plant through the ___. Then it travels up the ___.
questions.explanation: Water enters through the roots and travels up the stem, like water up a straw, to the leaves and flowers.

questions.title: Plants and Their Parts
questions.stem: Match each plant part to its job.
pairs: take in water from the soil
questions.explanation: Each part has a job: roots drink and hold, the stem carries water and holds the plant up, leaves make food, the flower makes seeds and the fruit protects them.

questions.title: Plants and Their Parts
questions.stem: Which of these does a plant need to grow well? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Plants need water, light and air, and also warmth and minerals from the soil. Sugar and rice do not feed a plant.

questions.title: Plants and Their Parts
questions.stem: Leaves use sunlight to make food for the plant.
questions.explanation: Leaves catch sunlight and use it to make food. That is why plants need light.

questions.title: Plants and Their Parts
questions.stem: A plant is not healthy. Which need is missing? Sort each sign.
items: The leaves droop and the soil is dry.
The seedling in the cupboard is thin and yellow.
New leaves are pale and weak.
The plant stopped growing in a very cold week.
A frosty night damaged the young plant.
questions.explanation: Drooping leaves and dry soil mean a plant needs water. Yellow, thin growth means it needs light. A plant that stops growing in the cold needs warmth.

questions.title: Plants and Their Parts
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to show how water gets to a leaf.
sequence: Rain soaks into the soil.
The roots take in the water.
The water travels up the stem.
The water reaches the leaves and flowers.
questions.explanation: Water starts in the soil. The roots take it in, the stem carries it up, and it reaches the leaves and flowers.

questions.title: Plants and Their Parts
questions.stem: Why does a plant need healthy roots?
questions.model_answer: Roots hold the plant in the soil and take in water for the plant.
questions.explanation: Roots do two jobs: they hold the plant in the soil and they take in water. A plant with damaged roots cannot drink and may fall over.

questions.title: Plants and Their Parts
questions.stem: A bean plant kept in a dark cupboard for a week will have strong, dark green leaves.
questions.explanation: Without light, leaves turn yellow and the plant becomes weak. Plants need light to make food.

questions.title: Plants and Their Parts
questions.stem: In April it is very hot. Mina's rooftop plants wilt at midday. What should Mina do?
options: Cover the plants with a black plastic sheet.
Put up a cloth for shade and water them in the morning.
Stop watering until the plants stand up again.
Move the pots into a dark room.
questions.explanation: Wilting means the plants are losing water in the heat. A cloth gives shade and morning watering gives them water, so they recover.

questions.title: Plants and Their Parts
questions.stem: Sumi's tomato seedling is in a pot outside. A very cold night is coming. What is the best thing to do?
options: Leave the pot outside and water it more.
Put the pot in a dark cupboard.
Bring the pot inside where it is warmer.
questions.explanation: Young plants can be damaged or stop growing when it is too cold. Bringing the pot inside keeps it warmer, and it still needs light the next day.

questions.title: Plants and Their Parts
questions.stem: Joy keeps his plant in a dark store room. He says, 'I water it every day, so it will grow strong and green.' Is Joy right?
questions.explanation: Water is not enough. The plant also needs light to make food, so it will become yellow and weak in the dark.

questions.title: Plants and Their Parts
questions.stem: Nadia has a plant in a pot. Which things will help it grow well? Choose all that are right.
options: put it where it gets sunlight
keep its roots in good soil
keep it in a dark cupboard
questions.explanation: A plant grows well with light, water and healthy roots in good soil. Pulling off its leaves, or keeping it in the dark, would harm it.

questions.title: Plants and Their Parts
questions.stem: A plant that does not get enough water droops, which we call wilting.
questions.explanation: Wilting means drooping because the plant needs water. After watering, a wilted plant often stands up again.

questions.title: Plants and Their Parts
questions.stem: Without ___, a plant turns yellow and weak. Without ___, it wilts.
questions.explanation: A plant needs light to make food, so it turns yellow and weak in the dark. Without water it droops and wilts.

questions.title: Plants and Their Parts
questions.stem: Class 2B grew two bean plants with the same water (example data). Plant A, by the window, was 12 cm tall with green leaves. Plant B, in the dark, was 15 cm tall with yellow leaves. Rafi says, 'Plant B is taller, so it is healthier.' What is the best reply?
options: Plant B is yellow and weak, so it is not healthy even though it is taller.
Plant B is right, because taller plants are always healthier.
Plant A is shorter, so it must have had less water.
Both plants are the same because they had the same water.
questions.explanation: Plant B grew tall and thin, as if reaching for light, but its leaves are yellow and it is weak. Height alone does not show that a plant is healthy.

questions.title: Plants and Their Parts
questions.stem: Mina plants the same bean seeds in three pots. Pot 1: sunny shelf, 1 cup of water a day. Pot 2: dark cupboard, 1 cup of water a day. Pot 3: dark cupboard, no water. Which two pots should she compare to find out whether plants need light?
questions.explanation: To test light, only light should change. Pots 1 and 2 get the same water, but one has light and one does not.

questions.title: Plants and Their Parts
questions.stem: Why must the bean plant in the dark cupboard get the same amount of water as the plant by the window?
questions.model_answer: So the only thing that is different is light. If the water was different too, we would not know which one caused the change.
questions.explanation: If the water was different as well, we could not tell whether light or water caused the difference. A fair test changes only one thing.

questions.title: Plants and Their Parts
questions.stem: Farmers in Bangladesh plant rice when the monsoon rains come. Why is this a good time?
options: Rice grows best in the dark.
The rain gives the rice plant its seeds.
Rice plants do not need sunlight.
There is lots of water and the weather is warm.
questions.explanation: Rice needs plenty of water, and the monsoon season is warm and wet. Plants grow well when they have water and the right temperature.

questions.title: Plants and Their Parts
questions.stem: Plants grow best at the right ___: not too hot and not too cold.
questions.explanation: Temperature affects growth. In very hot weather plants can wilt, and in very cold weather they may stop growing.

questions.title: Living and Non-Living Things
questions.stem: Which of these is a living thing?
questions.explanation: A cat moves, breathes, feeds, grows and has young. A chair, a stone and a pencil do none of these things, so they are non-living.

questions.title: Living and Non-Living Things
questions.stem: Sort the pictures into living and non-living things.
questions.explanation: Cats, sunflowers and ants are living. They grow, feed and have young. A chair, a football, a spoon and a pencil are non-living.

questions.title: Living and Non-Living Things
questions.stem: Look at the pond. Which number shows a non-living thing?
questions.image_alt: A pond scene with eight things numbered 1 to 8.
questions.explanation: Number 6 is a rock. A rock does not eat, grow or have young. The duck (3), fish (4) and frog (8) are living.

questions.title: Living and Non-Living Things
questions.stem: Look at the pond. Which numbers show living things? Choose all that are right.
questions.image_alt: A pond scene with eight things numbered 1 to 8.
questions.explanation: The duck (3), fish (4), water plants (7) and frog (8) are living. The Sun (1) and the water (5) are non-living.

questions.title: Living and Non-Living Things
questions.stem: Which animal has feathers?
questions.explanation: A parrot is covered in feathers. A cat has fur and a fish has scales.

questions.title: Living and Non-Living Things
questions.stem: Look at each animal. Sort them by what covers its body.
questions.explanation: Cats and goats have fur. Ducks, parrots and owls have feathers. Fish, snakes and crocodiles have scales.

questions.title: Living and Non-Living Things
questions.stem: A living thing moves, breathes, feeds, grows and has ___.
questions.explanation: Living things have young. A hen lays eggs and a mango tree makes seeds.

questions.title: Living and Non-Living Things
questions.stem: Match each thing that living things do to an example.
questions.explanation: A living thing moves, breathes, grows, senses and has young. Each example shows one of these.

questions.title: Living and Non-Living Things
questions.stem: All living things grow.
questions.explanation: Growing is one of the things all living things do. A kitten grows into a cat and a seedling grows into a plant.

questions.title: Living and Non-Living Things
questions.stem: A car is a living thing because it moves and needs fuel.
questions.explanation: A car moves and uses fuel, but it does not grow, breathe or have young. A living thing does all of these things, so a car is non-living.

questions.title: Living and Non-Living Things
questions.stem: Which of these do living things do? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Living things grow, breathe and get rid of waste. Not every living thing can fly or swim.

questions.title: Living and Non-Living Things
questions.stem: A toy robot can move and make sounds. Is it a living thing? Explain.
questions.model_answer: No. It cannot grow, eat, breathe or have young, so it is not living.
questions.explanation: A robot only moves because it is built and has batteries. It cannot grow, eat, breathe or have young, so it is non-living.

questions.title: Living and Non-Living Things
questions.stem: Which of these things was once alive?
questions.explanation: A wooden spoon is made from wood, which comes from a tree. It is now non-living, but it was once alive. Metal, plastic and glass were never alive.

questions.title: Living and Non-Living Things
questions.stem: Scientists sort animals into groups by looking at their…
options: features you can see, like fur or wings
questions.explanation: We sort living things by features we can see, such as fur, feathers, scales, wings or legs.

questions.title: Living and Non-Living Things
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to sort a set of animals into two groups.
sequence: Look closely at all the animals.
Choose one feature, such as having legs.
Put animals with that feature in one group.
Put the other animals in a second group.
Say why you made the groups.
questions.explanation: To sort, look closely, choose a feature, put animals with it in one group, put the rest in the other group, and explain your reason.

questions.title: Living and Non-Living Things
questions.stem: Imran keeps dry beans in wet cotton wool for three days. Tiny roots and shoots appear. What does this tell us about the beans?
options: They are living, because they grew roots and shoots.
They are only soaking up water, like a sponge.
They are non-living, because they are dry.
questions.explanation: Growing is a sign of life. The beans grew roots and shoots, so they are living, even though dry seeds look still.

questions.title: Living and Non-Living Things
questions.stem: Mina sees a thin brown thing on a leaf. It looks like a twig, but she thinks it might be an insect. What is the best way to find out?
options: Watch it carefully for a while.
Decide it is non-living because it is still.
Poke it hard with a stick.
Pick it up and squeeze it.
questions.explanation: To tell if something is living, we watch for signs such as moving, feeding or growing. We stay safe and do not hurt it. A living thing may be still for a while.

questions.title: Living and Non-Living Things
questions.stem: Nadia watches the river flow past. She says, 'The river water is living because it moves.' Is she right?
questions.explanation: Water moves, but it does not breathe, feed, grow or have young. Moving is not enough to be living.

questions.title: Living and Non-Living Things
questions.stem: Tanvir sits by a village pond. He sees ducks, stones, lotus flowers, an old boat and a fish. Which of these are living? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Ducks, lotus flowers and fish are living. Stones and an old boat are non-living.

questions.title: Living and Non-Living Things
questions.stem: Sort these animals into groups by looking at their legs.
questions.explanation: Cats, goats, ants and ducks have legs. Snakes, fish, snails and worms have no legs.

questions.title: Living and Non-Living Things
questions.stem: Why is a plant a living thing?
questions.explanation: A plant grows, makes its own food, and makes seeds to have young. Being green or having a name does not make something living.

questions.title: Living and Non-Living Things
questions.stem: Scientists sort living things into groups by looking at their ___, such as fur, feathers or wings.
questions.explanation: A feature is something you can see. We use features to sort living things into groups.

questions.title: Living and Non-Living Things
questions.stem: Class 2C counted things in the school garden (example data): trees 5, birds 8, ants 20, butterflies 3, stones 4 and benches 2. How many living things did they count in all?
questions.explanation: The living things are the trees, birds, ants and butterflies: 5 + 8 + 20 + 3 = 36. Stones and benches are non-living, so they are not counted.

questions.title: Living and Non-Living Things
questions.stem: Mystery object: it does not move, breathe or grow. It once was part of a tree. Which could it be?
questions.explanation: A dry leaf was once part of a living tree, but it is no longer alive. A sleeping cat, a young mango tree and a seed in wet soil are all still living.

questions.title: Living and Non-Living Things
questions.stem: A seed does not move, eat or breathe in a way we can see. Why is it still a living thing?
questions.model_answer: A seed is living because it can grow into a new plant when it gets water and warmth.
questions.explanation: A seed is alive. When it gets water and warmth, it grows into a new plant, and growing is a sign of life.

questions.title: Living and Non-Living Things
questions.stem: Look at the pond. Which number shows a non-living thing that gives light and heat?
questions.image_alt: A pond scene with eight things numbered 1 to 8.
questions.explanation: Number 1 is the Sun. It gives light and heat, but it is not a living thing. It does not breathe, feed, grow or have young.

questions.title: Life Cycles and Growth
questions.stem: A chick hatches from an…
questions.explanation: Chickens lay eggs, and chicks hatch from them. A chick grows into a hen, and the hen lays eggs again.

questions.title: Life Cycles and Growth
questions.stem: Match each young animal to its parent.
questions.explanation: Young animals have special names: a chick grows into a hen, a tadpole into a frog, a caterpillar into a butterfly, a calf into a cow and a kitten into a cat.

questions.title: Life Cycles and Growth
questions.stem: Put the pictures in order, from youngest to oldest.
questions.explanation: People grow from baby to child to adult to older adult. Children grow taller and heavier, and learn to walk, talk and read.

questions.title: Life Cycles and Growth
questions.stem: Look at the frog life cycle. What stage comes just after the tadpole?
questions.image_alt: The life cycle of a frog drawn as a circle of four labelled stages.
questions.explanation: A tadpole grows legs and becomes a froglet. The froglet grows into an adult frog.

questions.title: Life Cycles and Growth
questions.stem: Look at the butterfly life cycle. What does the caterpillar change into?
questions.image_alt: The life cycle of a butterfly drawn as a circle of four labelled stages.
questions.explanation: The caterpillar eats and grows, then turns into a chrysalis (pupa). An adult butterfly comes out of the chrysalis.

questions.title: Life Cycles and Growth
questions.stem: Look at the picture. Put the chicken life cycle in order, starting with the egg.
questions.image_alt: The life cycle of a chicken drawn as a circle of four labelled stages.
sequence: egg
hatching
chick
adult hen
questions.explanation: A hen lays an egg. The chick hatches, grows and becomes an adult hen, which can lay eggs again.

questions.title: Life Cycles and Growth
questions.stem: Look at the frog life cycle. Which two stages live only in water?
questions.image_alt: The life cycle of a frog drawn as a circle of four labelled stages.
questions.explanation: Frog eggs (frogspawn) and tadpoles need pond water. The froglet starts to live on land as well.

questions.title: Life Cycles and Growth
questions.stem: Which animal starts its life as a tadpole?
questions.explanation: A tadpole hatches from a frog's egg and lives in water. It grows legs and becomes a frog.

questions.title: Life Cycles and Growth
questions.stem: As a child grows, they get ___ and heavier.
questions.explanation: Children grow taller and heavier. Most children grow about 5 to 6 cm taller every year.

questions.title: Life Cycles and Growth
questions.stem: A baby human looks like a small person, but a tadpole looks very different from an adult frog.
questions.explanation: People do not change shape as they grow. A tadpole has a tail and lives in water. It changes shape, grows legs and becomes a frog.

questions.title: Life Cycles and Growth
questions.stem: Hilsa fish lay their eggs in rivers.
questions.explanation: In Bangladesh, hilsa lay their eggs in rivers. The baby fish grow in the river and then swim to the sea.

questions.title: Life Cycles and Growth
questions.stem: Which of these happen as a tadpole grows into a frog? Choose all that are right.
options: It can live on land too.
questions.explanation: The tadpole grows legs, its tail gets shorter and it begins to live on land too. It does not grow feathers or turn into a fish.

questions.title: Life Cycles and Growth
questions.stem: How does each young animal begin its life? Sort them.
questions.explanation: Chicks, tadpoles, caterpillars and baby turtles hatch from eggs. Calves, kittens and human babies are born from their mothers.

questions.title: Life Cycles and Growth
questions.stem: Put the sea turtle life cycle in order.
sequence: The mother lays eggs in the sand.
Baby turtles hatch.
The babies swim in the sea.
They grow into adults.
questions.explanation: A mother turtle lays eggs in the sand. The babies hatch, swim to the sea and grow into adults.

questions.title: Life Cycles and Growth
questions.stem: Where should a mother butterfly lay her eggs?
options: on a leaf the caterpillars can eat
questions.explanation: Butterfly eggs are laid on leaves, so the caterpillars can eat the leaves when they hatch.

questions.title: Life Cycles and Growth
questions.stem: A ___ is the place where an animal finds food, water and shelter.
questions.explanation: A habitat is an animal's home. Different stages of an animal's life may need different habitats.

questions.title: Life Cycles and Growth
questions.stem: Why does a frog lay its eggs in a pond, not on dry land?
questions.model_answer: The tadpoles need water to live and swim, so the eggs must be in the pond.
questions.explanation: Frog eggs hatch into tadpoles. Tadpoles live in water and cannot live on dry land.

questions.title: Life Cycles and Growth
questions.stem: Volunteers on a beach at night see baby turtles walking towards bright lights on the road, not towards the sea. What is the best thing for people to do?
options: Switch off bright lights and keep the beach dark and clean.
Shine bright torches at them to guide them.
Leave rubbish on the beach so they can hide.
Bring the babies home to look after them.
questions.explanation: Baby turtles can follow bright lights and lose their way. Keeping the beach dark and clean helps them find the sea.

questions.title: Life Cycles and Growth
questions.stem: Rafi's hen has hatched six chicks. It is a cold night. Where should the chicks stay?
options: on a cold floor by the door
under their mother in a warm, dry nest
questions.explanation: Chicks need a warm nest and their mother to keep them warm and safe.

questions.title: Life Cycles and Growth
questions.stem: Anika finds frogspawn (jelly-like frog eggs) in a ditch near her school. She says, 'The eggs will hatch into tadpoles, so the ditch must not dry up.' Is Anika right?
questions.explanation: Tadpoles live and swim in water. If the ditch dried up, the tadpoles could not survive.

questions.title: Life Cycles and Growth
questions.stem: Class 2A wants a school pond where frogs can grow up. Which things would help? Choose all that are right.
options: keep rubbish out of the pond
plant water plants and grass around it
questions.explanation: Frogs need water for eggs and tadpoles, a clean place, and plants for shelter and food. A pond filled with sand or one that dries out cannot be a habitat.

questions.title: Life Cycles and Growth
questions.stem: Raju measured his height every year (example data): age 6: 116 cm, age 7: 122 cm, age 8: 126 cm, age 9: 131 cm. In which year did he grow the most?
options: He grew the same amount each year.
questions.explanation: Between 6 and 7 he grew 6 cm. Between 7 and 8 he grew 4 cm, and between 8 and 9 he grew 5 cm. So he grew the most from age 6 to age 7.

questions.title: Life Cycles and Growth
questions.stem: Most children grow about 5 to 6 cm taller every year. Tuli is 120 cm tall now. About how tall will she be in 2 years?
questions.explanation: In 2 years she grows about 10 to 12 cm. 120 + 10 = 130 and 120 + 12 = 132, so about 131 cm is the best answer.

questions.title: Life Cycles and Growth
questions.stem: Sumi wrote the frog life cycle as: egg, froglet, tadpole, adult frog. What did she get wrong?
options: There should be no adult frog.
The tadpole and froglet are in the wrong order.
questions.explanation: The tadpole stage comes before the froglet. A tadpole grows legs and turns into a froglet, then an adult frog.

questions.title: Life Cycles and Growth
questions.stem: How is the way a baby human grows up different from the way a tadpole grows up?
questions.model_answer: A baby human looks like a small person and just gets bigger. A tadpole looks very different: it lives in water and changes shape as it grows legs and a frog body.
questions.explanation: A baby human already has the shape of a small person and just gets bigger. A tadpole lives in water and changes shape, growing legs and losing its tail.

questions.title: Life Cycles and Growth
questions.stem: Where does each young animal or egg need to be? Sort them.
questions.explanation: Frog eggs and tadpoles need water. Butterfly eggs and caterpillars need leaves to eat. Chicks and eggs need a warm nest.

questions.title: The Human Body: Parts and Organs
questions.stem: Which organ takes in air when you breathe?
questions.explanation: The lungs take in air. The heart pumps blood, the liver cleans blood, and the stomach mashes up food.

questions.title: The Human Body: Parts and Organs
questions.stem: Look at the picture of the body. Which number shows the knee?
questions.image_alt: Outline of a child with body parts numbered 1 to 11.
questions.explanation: Number 10 is the knee. It is a joint in the middle of the leg, so your leg can bend there.

questions.title: The Human Body: Parts and Organs
questions.stem: Look at the picture of the body. Which number shows the elbow?
questions.image_alt: Outline of a child with body parts numbered 1 to 11.
questions.explanation: Number 5 is the elbow. It is the joint in the middle of the arm that lets you bend your arm.

questions.title: The Human Body: Parts and Organs
questions.stem: Look at the skeleton. Which number shows the bone that protects the brain?
questions.image_alt: A human skeleton with some bones numbered.
questions.explanation: Number 1 is the skull. It is a hard bone shell around the brain. The ribs (2) protect the heart and lungs.

questions.title: The Human Body: Parts and Organs
questions.stem: Look at the skeleton. Which number shows the bones that make a cage to protect the heart and lungs?
questions.image_alt: A human skeleton with some bones numbered.
questions.explanation: Number 2 is the ribs. They curve around the chest like a cage and protect the heart and lungs.

questions.title: The Human Body: Parts and Organs
questions.stem: Look at the arm. Which number shows the joint, where two bones meet and bend?
questions.image_alt: An arm with a bone, two muscles and the elbow joint numbered 1 to 4.
questions.explanation: Number 4 is the elbow joint. A joint is where two bones meet, and it lets the arm bend.

questions.title: The Human Body: Parts and Organs
questions.stem: Joints are where two bones meet and bend. Look at the body. Which numbers show joints? Choose all that are right.
questions.image_alt: Outline of a child with body parts numbered 1 to 11.
questions.explanation: The elbow (5) and the knee (10) are joints that bend. The head (1), chest (7) and foot (11) are not joints.

questions.title: The Human Body: Parts and Organs
questions.stem: Match each picture to its job.
pairs: holds you up and gives you shape
questions.explanation: The brain controls the body and helps you think. The heart pumps blood. The lungs take in air. Bones hold you up and give you your shape.

questions.title: The Human Body: Parts and Organs
questions.stem: Match each organ to its job.
pairs: take goodness from food into your blood
controls your body and helps you think
questions.explanation: The stomach mashes food. The intestines take goodness from food into the blood. The liver cleans blood, the bladder stores urine, and the brain is the controller.

questions.title: The Human Body: Parts and Organs
questions.stem: The ___ is the bone that protects your brain.
questions.explanation: The skull is a hard shell of bone around the brain. It protects the brain from bumps.

questions.title: The Human Body: Parts and Organs
questions.stem: Muscles are joined to bones. When a muscle pulls, the bone moves.
questions.explanation: Muscles pull on bones to make them move. Bones and muscles work together so we can walk, run and kick.

questions.title: The Human Body: Parts and Organs
questions.stem: Your heart only beats when you are awake.
questions.explanation: Your heart beats all day and all night, about 100 times every minute, even when you are asleep.

questions.title: The Human Body: Parts and Organs
questions.stem: Which of these are organs inside your body? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: The heart, lungs and stomach are organs inside the body. The knee and the hand are outside parts of the body.

questions.title: The Human Body: Parts and Organs
