It sinks, because lift is bigger than weight.
questions.explanation: Lift is 10 000 N bigger than weight, so the plane rises. Thrust equals drag, so its forward speed stays steady.

questions.title: Floating and Flying
questions.stem: A steel nail sinks, but a huge steel ship floats. Explain why.
questions.model_answer: The ship is hollow and full of air, so it is light for its size and displaces a lot of water, which gives enough upthrust to hold up its weight. The solid nail is too dense.
questions.explanation: What matters is the shape, not just the material. The hollow ship pushes aside so much water that the upthrust equals its weight. The small solid nail displaces too little water.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: What do we call a complete path that electricity flows round?
questions.explanation: A circuit is a complete path with no gaps. Electricity flows from one end of the cell, through the wires and components, and back to the other end.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Match each circuit part to its job.
questions.explanation: Scientists give each component a job and a symbol. The cell is the energy store; the lamp, buzzer and motor use the energy; the switch controls the circuit.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: What happens to the lamp in a series circuit when you make each change?
items: add a second lamp in the same loop
take one wire out of the loop
questions.explanation: More cells push harder, so the lamp is brighter. A second lamp shares the push, and a longer wire lets less electricity through, so the lamp is dimmer. Any gap stops the electricity completely.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Electricity can flow round a circuit that has a gap in it.
questions.explanation: Electricity needs a complete loop. A gap, such as an open switch or a loose wire, makes the lamp go out.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Materials that let electricity flow through them are called ___. Materials that do not let it flow are called ___.
questions.explanation: Most metals are conductors. Plastic, rubber, wood and glass are insulators.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Why is the inside of an electric cable made of copper?
options: Copper stops shocks reaching our hands.
Copper is a good insulator for wires.
questions.explanation: Copper lets electricity flow very easily. It is the plastic cover, not the copper, that stops electricity reaching our hands.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: A bulb is in a circuit with a gap. Which objects would make the bulb light if you joined the gap with them? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Steel, aluminium and copper are metals, so they conduct and complete the circuit. Plastic, wood and rubber are insulators, so the gap stays.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to find out how wire length changes the brightness of a bulb.
sequence: Build a circuit with a cell, a bulb and a long thin wire with a crocodile clip.
Clip at 10 cm and measure the brightness with a light meter.
Move the clip to 20 cm and measure again, then 30, 40 and 50 cm.
Draw a line graph of brightness against wire length.
Describe the pattern in the graph.
questions.explanation: First set up the circuit, then take the measurements, then draw the graph, and last describe the pattern you see.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: A ___ opens or closes a gap in a circuit, and a ___ cuts off the electricity if too much flows.
questions.explanation: A switch lets us turn things on and off. Fuses and circuit breakers are safety switches that stop wires getting hot and starting a fire.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Why is an electric cable made with copper wire inside and a plastic cover outside?
questions.model_answer: Copper conducts electricity well, and the plastic is an insulator that keeps the electricity in and protects us from shocks.
questions.explanation: The copper lets electricity flow along the cable. The plastic does not let it flow, so people who touch the cable stay safe.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: A fuse or circuit breaker switches off the electricity if too much flows, before the wires get hot.
questions.explanation: Fuses and circuit breakers are safety switches. Without them, overheated wires could start a fire.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: In 2000, about 32 out of every 100 homes in Bangladesh had electricity. In 2020 it was about 96 out of 100. The rise was ___ homes out of 100.
questions.explanation: 96 - 32 = 64. The figures are approximate, from World Bank data on access to electricity.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Why is the lamp off in this circuit?
questions.image_alt: A circuit with a cell, a lamp and an open switch; the lamp is off.
options: The lamp is too close to the cell.
The wires are the wrong colour.
The switch is open, so there is a gap.
The cell is too small to push electricity.
questions.explanation: An open switch is a gap in the loop. Electricity cannot flow round, so the lamp stays off. Closing the switch would complete the circuit.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Compare this circuit with one that has the same cell and only one lamp. What is different about the lamps here?
questions.image_alt: A circuit with one cell and two lamps in one loop. Both lamps are on.
options: Both lamps are the same brightness as one lamp alone.
questions.explanation: The cell has to push electricity through two lamps, so it is shared. Each lamp gets less and looks dimmer than a single lamp.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: This model shows tiny particles moving round a circuit. What does it tell us?
questions.image_alt: Tiny particles flowing round a complete circuit loop.
options: They are used up in the lamp.
They flow from the cell to the lamp and stop.
They flow all the way round the complete loop.
questions.explanation: In a circuit the flow goes all the way round. The lamp changes the energy into light, but the flow itself is not used up.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Sort these pictures into conductors and insulators.
questions.explanation: Keys, coins and steel paper clips are made of metal, so they conduct. Plastic, glass and wood are insulators.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Match each picture to its job.
pairs: tells drivers when to stop and go
moves air to keep us cool
gives light to read at night
charges from a plug or solar panel
questions.explanation: Electrical systems are in homes, schools and the community. Each has a source, wires and a part that does a job.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Tuli has just washed her hands and they are wet. She needs to plug in her phone charger. What should she do?
options: Plug it in quickly while her hands are wet.
Wrap a wet cloth round the plug.
Push the plug in with a metal spoon.
questions.explanation: Water can conduct electricity, so wet hands near a socket can give a dangerous shock. Always dry your hands first and never push a metal object into a socket.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Raju's kite gets caught on a power line. What should he do?
options: Climb the pole to reach it.
Pull the string hard to get it down.
Leave it there and tell an adult.
Throw a stick at the wire.
questions.explanation: Power lines carry very strong electricity, and a wet string or stick can let it travel down to you. Never touch the kite and always tell an adult.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Lina plugs a fan, a TV, a heater and three chargers into one socket with an adaptor. Why is this dangerous?
options: Too much electricity can overheat the wires and start a fire.
The electricity will stop flowing to every device.
The electricity will leak out of the unused holes.
The devices will all run too fast.
questions.explanation: Each device draws electricity. If too much flows through one socket the wires get hot, which can cause a fire. Use fewer plugs in each socket.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: A cable has a cracked plastic cover and the copper wire is showing. Anika says it is safe to keep using it if she does not touch the wire. Is she right?
questions.explanation: Bare copper can give a deadly shock if anything touches it, and it can start a fire. A damaged cable must be replaced by an adult.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Nadia's class wants to save electricity at school. Which actions would help? Choose all that are right.
options: switch off fans and lights at break
leave the computers on all night
unplug chargers when they are not needed
run the fans in empty rooms
questions.explanation: Using less electricity, or using it more efficiently, saves energy. Leaving things on when nobody uses them wastes it.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Why is it dangerous to use a hair dryer with wet hands in a bathroom?
questions.model_answer: Water that is dirty or salty can conduct electricity, so electricity could flow through your body and give a dangerous shock.
questions.explanation: Normal tap water has dissolved salts, so it conducts. Wet skin lets electricity pass into your body, which can be deadly.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: In the simulation, what happens to the bulb when you open the switch?

sim.task: Open Circuit Construction Kit. Drag a battery, a light bulb, a switch and wires onto the board to make one complete loop. Close the switch and watch the bulb. Then open the switch.

options: The bulb gets a little dimmer.
questions.explanation: Opening the switch makes a gap in the loop, so no electricity flows and the bulb goes out. Closing it lights the bulb again.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: In the simulation, which objects made the bulb light when you put them in the circuit? Choose all that are right.

sim.task: Open Circuit Construction Kit and choose the Lab screen. Build a loop with a battery and a bulb, leaving a gap. Put each object in the gap one at a time: coin, paper clip, eraser, dollar bill. Watch the bulb each time.

questions.explanation: The coin and the paper clip are metal, so they conduct electricity and the bulb lights. The eraser and the paper money are insulators.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: In the simulation, you put a second bulb in the same loop as the first. What happens to the first bulb?

sim.task: Open Circuit Construction Kit. Build a loop with one battery and one bulb and note how bright it is. Then add a second bulb into the same loop (one after the other). Compare the brightness.

questions.explanation: The battery has to push electricity through both bulbs, so each one is dimmer than a single bulb on its own.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Class 4C measured the brightness of a bulb (in lux) as they made the wire in the circuit longer: 10 cm = 200, 20 cm = 160, 30 cm = 130, 40 cm = 110, 50 cm = 95. What brightness would you expect for 60 cm?
questions.explanation: The bulb gets dimmer as the wire gets longer, but the drops get smaller each time (40, 30, 20, 15). The next drop would be about 12 or 13, giving about 82 lux.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Joy tests whether wire length changes bulb brightness. Test 1 uses a 10 cm wire and a new cell. Test 2 uses a 30 cm wire and an old cell. Why is her test unfair?
options: She measured the brightness with a light meter.
She changed two things, the wire length and the cell.
She used a bulb in both tests.
questions.explanation: In a fair test only one thing is changed. Joy changed the wire and the cell, so she cannot tell which one made the difference.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Design a burglar alarm for a box. A buzzer must sound when someone opens the lid. Explain how your circuit works.
questions.model_answer: Use a cell, a buzzer and a switch made of two foil strips. When the lid opens the foil strips touch, the circuit is complete, and the buzzer sounds.
questions.explanation: The alarm needs a switch that closes when the lid opens. Closing the switch completes the circuit so electricity flows to the buzzer.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.stem: Raju joins one wire from the top of a cell to the base of a bulb. Nothing else touches the bulb or the bottom of the cell. Will the bulb light?
options: Yes, electricity only needs to leave the top of the cell.
Yes, the bulb lights dimly because the wire is short.
No, because a single wire is too short to carry any electricity.
No, there is no complete loop back to the cell.
questions.explanation: A bulb needs a complete loop: out of one end of the cell and back to the other. One wire makes a gap, so electricity cannot flow and the bulb stays off.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: Which of these would a magnet attract?
questions.explanation: Iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are magnetic materials. Copper and aluminium are metals but are not magnetic, and plastic is not magnetic either.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: Sort these objects into those a magnet attracts and those it does not.
questions.explanation: Only iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are attracted. Aluminium, copper and gold are metals but they are not magnetic.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: Match each key word to its meaning.
pairs: the two ends of a magnet, where the force is strongest
a small magnet that swings to point north
the space around a magnet where it has an effect
a magnet made when electricity flows in a coil
questions.explanation: Every magnet has two poles. A compass needle is a small magnet. The field is the space where the magnet can act, and an electromagnet works only while electricity flows.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: All metals are magnetic.
questions.explanation: Only some metals, such as iron, steel and nickel, are magnetic. A magnet will pick up a steel paper clip but not an aluminium can or a copper wire.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: The ends of a magnet are called ___. Like poles ___ each other.
questions.explanation: A magnet has a north pole and a south pole. Like poles (N and N, or S and S) repel; unlike poles attract.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: A magnet can pull a paper clip through a sheet of paper without touching the clip.
questions.explanation: Magnetism is a non-contact force. It acts through the space around the magnet and passes through paper, plastic, water and even your hand.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to make and use an electromagnet.
sequence: Wrap a long wire many times around an iron nail.
Join the ends of the wire to a battery.
Electricity flows through the coil and the nail becomes a magnet.
Pick up some paper clips with the nail.
Disconnect the battery so the clips drop.
questions.explanation: The coil and the nail are made first, then the electricity is switched on. When the electricity is switched off the magnetism disappears and the clips fall.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: Which changes would make an electromagnet stronger? Choose all that are right.
options: use a wooden stick instead of the iron nail
questions.explanation: More coils, more cells and a thicker iron core all make the magnet stronger. With no electricity there is no magnetism, and wood is not magnetic.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: Why can a magnet pick up a steel paper clip but not an aluminium can?
questions.model_answer: Steel contains iron, which is a magnetic material, but aluminium is not magnetic.
questions.explanation: Magnets attract only iron, steel, nickel and cobalt. Aluminium is a metal but it is not a magnetic material.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: Why does a compass needle swing round to point north?
options: Earth behaves like a giant magnet.
The Sun pulls the needle towards the north.
The wind always blows the needle northwards.
The north is the lightest direction to turn.
questions.explanation: A compass needle is a small magnet. The Earth acts like a huge magnet, so the needle lines up with it and points north.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: A big magnet is always stronger than a small magnet.
questions.explanation: Size does not tell you the strength. Some tiny magnets are very strong and some big ones are weak. We test strength by counting paper clips or sheets of paper.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: An electromagnet is made from a coil of ___ wrapped around an iron ___.
questions.explanation: Electricity flowing through the coil of wire turns the iron nail into a magnet. Switch off the electricity and the magnetism disappears.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: Mina turns the right-hand magnet in the top pair round, so that two N poles face each other. What will the magnets do?
questions.image_alt: Two pairs of bar magnets. In one pair S faces N and they attract. In the other pair N faces N and they repel.
options: They will stay exactly where they are.
They will push each other apart.
They will lose their poles for a while.
questions.explanation: Two like poles (N and N) repel. The magnets only attract when a north pole faces a south pole.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: Which of these would a magnet pick up?
questions.explanation: A steel paper clip contains iron, so a magnet attracts it. Wood, plastic and glass are not magnetic.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: Sort the pictures into things a magnet attracts and things it does not.
questions.explanation: Nuts, bolts, pins and needles are made of steel, which contains iron. Feathers, wood and glass are not magnetic.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: Match each picture to how it uses magnets or electricity.
pairs: finds the way by pointing north
uses a magnet to make sound
questions.explanation: Compasses, speakers, motors and electric bells all use magnets. Many everyday machines depend on them.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: Fishers on the Bay of Bengal use one of these to find north. Which one?
questions.explanation: A compass has a magnetic needle that points north. Torches, keys and candles cannot show direction.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: Rafi has a sack of mixed steel cans and aluminium cans for recycling. How can he separate them quickly?
options: Use a magnet to pick up steel cans.
Drop each can into a bucket of water.
Shine a torch on every single can.
Weigh each can on a kitchen scale.
questions.explanation: A magnet attracts the steel cans but not the aluminium ones. This is how recycling plants sort cans.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: A scrap yard crane uses a huge electromagnet, not an ordinary magnet, to move iron and steel. Explain why.
questions.model_answer: An electromagnet can be switched off to drop the scrap where it is needed, but an ordinary magnet would never let go.
questions.explanation: An electromagnet works only while electricity flows. Switch it on to pick up the scrap, and off to drop it onto the truck.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: A fisher is far out on the Bay of Bengal on a cloudy night and cannot see the stars. How can a compass help?
options: It shows how deep the water is below the boat.
It shows which way is north.
It warns him when a cyclone is coming.
It tells him where the fish are swimming.
questions.explanation: The magnetic needle always swings to point north, so the fisher can work out which way to travel even when he cannot see landmarks.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: Little Sumi finds a tiny round magnet and puts it in her mouth. This is safe because the magnet is so small.
questions.explanation: Never let small children swallow magnets. They can be very dangerous inside the body. Tell an adult at once.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: Tuli's electromagnet lifts only 4 paper clips, but she wants it to lift 10. What should she change?
options: Swap the iron nail for a long wooden stick.
Wrap more coils of wire round the nail.
Let the wire hang loosely off the nail.
questions.explanation: More coils make the electromagnet stronger. Fewer cells, a wooden core or a loose wire would make it weaker.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: In the simulation, you add more loops of wire to the coil. What happens to the electromagnet?

sim.task: Open Magnets and Electromagnets and choose the Electromagnet screen. Switch on the battery. Look at the field meter and compass. Then increase the number of loops in the coil and watch again.

questions.explanation: More loops make a stronger magnetic field, so the electromagnet can pull harder. This matches what happens with a real coil and nail.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: In the simulation, you reverse the battery of the electromagnet. What happens to its poles?

sim.task: Open Magnets and Electromagnets and choose the Electromagnet screen. Switch on the battery and put the compass near one end of the coil. Note where the needle points. Then reverse the battery and watch the compass.

options: The poles stay exactly where they were.
The north and south poles swap ends.
questions.explanation: Reversing the battery reverses the direction of the electricity, so the north and south poles swap. You can see it from the compass needle turning round.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: In the simulation, you flip the bar magnet over. What does the compass needle do?

sim.task: Open Magnet and Compass. Move the compass near the bar magnet and watch the needle. Then flip the bar magnet over and watch the needle again.

options: It stays pointing in exactly the same way.
It spins round and round for ever.
It flips round to point the other way.
questions.explanation: The compass needle is a small magnet that lines up with the magnetic field. Flipping the bar magnet flips the field, so the needle turns round.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: In the simulation, with the battery voltage turned down to zero, the coil still works as a strong magnet.

sim.task: Open Magnets and Electromagnets and choose the Electromagnet screen. Set the battery voltage to its highest and look at the field meter. Then turn the voltage down to zero and look again.

questions.explanation: No electricity flowing means no magnetism in an electromagnet. The field meter reads almost zero, and the compass needle is not pulled.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: Class 4B counted how many sheets of paper each magnet could pull a paper clip through (mean of 3 tries): bar magnet 13, horseshoe magnet 18, fridge magnet 3, small round magnet 21. Which statement does the data support?
options: The biggest magnet was the strongest.
The horseshoe magnet was the strongest of the four.
The fridge magnet was stronger than the bar magnet.
The small round magnet was the strongest.
questions.explanation: The small round magnet held the clip through the most sheets (21), so it was the strongest. The data do not show that bigger magnets are stronger.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: Raju tested an electromagnet (example results): 10 coils lifted 3 clips, 20 coils lifted 6 clips and 30 coils lifted 9 clips. With 40 coils it should lift about ___ clips.
questions.explanation: Every extra 10 coils lifts 3 more clips, so 40 coils should lift 9 + 3 = 12 clips. This is a prediction from the pattern, which we would then test.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: You have a magnet with N and S marked, and a second magnet with no labels. How can you find out which end of the second magnet is its north pole?
questions.model_answer: Bring the N pole of the labelled magnet near one end. If that end repels it, it is a north pole; if it attracts it, it is a south pole.
questions.explanation: Like poles repel and unlike poles attract. So an end that pushes the labelled N pole away must also be a north pole.

questions.title: Magnets and Electromagnets
questions.stem: Raju brings the N pole of his magnet near each end of a mystery bar. One end is attracted and the other end is pushed away. What must the bar be?
questions.explanation: Plain iron is attracted at both ends but is never pushed away. Only a magnet can repel another magnet's pole, so the bar is a magnet.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Energy is what makes things…
questions.explanation: You need energy to run and think, a fan needs it to spin and a lamp needs it to shine. We cannot see energy, but we can see what it does.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Match each example to the form of energy it shows.
questions.explanation: Moving things have kinetic energy. Food and fuels store chemical energy. A stretched band stores energy ready to be used.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Sort these energy sources into those that will run out and those that will not.
questions.explanation: Coal, oil and gas took millions of years to form and will run out. Sunlight, wind, flowing water and biogas can be used again and again.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Energy can be ___ from one form to another, and ___ from one object to another.
questions.explanation: When a fan spins, electrical energy is converted to kinetic energy. When a hot spoon warms your hand, heat is transferred from the spoon to you.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to show how a solar home system gives light.
sequence: Sunlight shines on the solar panel.
The panel changes the light into electrical energy.
Electricity flows along the wires.
The bulb changes the electricity into light and a little heat.
questions.explanation: Energy is tracked step by step: light, then electrical energy, then light again at the bulb, with some heat given off.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: What energy change happens in a solar panel?
questions.explanation: A solar panel catches sunlight and changes it into electrical energy. Many families in Bangladesh use solar home systems for lights and phone charging.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Match each device to the energy change it makes.
questions.explanation: Each device changes energy from one form to another, so we can show it as an energy chain.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Rubbing your hands together changes kinetic energy into heat.
questions.explanation: Your hands move (kinetic energy), and friction changes some of that movement into heat, so your hands feel warm.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: A hot spoon warms your hand. What is happening to the heat energy?
options: It is passed on to your hand.
It is made from nothing at all.
It is destroyed when it touches skin.
questions.explanation: Heat energy is transferred (passed on) from the hot spoon to your cooler hand. Energy is not destroyed or created.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Why do we say that almost all of our energy comes from the Sun? Give one example.
questions.model_answer: Plants use the Sun's light to make food, which gives us energy, and coal, oil and gas came from ancient plants.
questions.explanation: Plants store the Sun's energy in food. Fuels such as coal, oil and gas came from ancient plants, and wind and rain are driven by the Sun's heat.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Which action helps to save energy at home?
options: Leave the TV on while you sleep.
Switch off fans in empty rooms.
Keep the fridge door open longer.
questions.explanation: Using less electricity saves energy. Switching off fans, lights and TVs when nobody is using them is one of the easiest ways.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Which of these have stored (potential) energy? Choose all that are right.
options: a book on a high shelf
questions.explanation: Stored energy is waiting to be used. A rolling football and a flowing river are moving, so they have kinetic energy.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Some energy is always wasted as ___, which is why a bulb or a motor gets warm.
questions.explanation: No machine turns all its energy into useful work. Some always escapes as heat.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Sort these pictures by the main useful energy they give out.
questions.explanation: Bulbs and torches give out light, speakers and radios give out sound, and fans and cars move. Each one converts energy into a useful form.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Which picture shows a device that changes light from the Sun into electrical energy?
questions.explanation: A solar panel catches sunlight and changes it into electrical energy. A fan, a candle and a loudspeaker do different jobs.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Match each picture to the energy it stores or gives out.
pairs: has kinetic energy in moving air
questions.explanation: Food stores chemical energy, a fire gives out heat and light, a speaker gives out sound, and moving air has kinetic energy.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Put the pictures in order to follow the energy from the Sun to a bicycle ride.
questions.explanation: The Sun's light helps rice grow and stores chemical energy. We eat the rice, and our muscles change the chemical energy into the movement of the bicycle.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Which picture shows a device that changes electrical energy into sound?
questions.explanation: A loudspeaker turns electrical energy into sound. A bulb makes light, a fan makes movement, and a torch changes chemical energy in its cells to light.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: A family in a village makes biogas from cow dung. Why is biogas called a renewable source?
options: It took millions of years to form deep underground.
More gas can be made while the cows keep eating.
It comes from under the ground and is soon used up.
It is made from coal that has been cleaned.
questions.explanation: Cows eat grass and make dung all the time, so new gas can keep being made. Coal, oil and natural gas took millions of years to form and will run out.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: An old filament bulb gets very hot, but an LED bulb stays cool. Which one wastes more energy as heat?
questions.explanation: Much of the electrical energy in a filament bulb becomes heat instead of light. LEDs give the same light with much less electricity.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Sumi's village home has a small solar panel on the roof that lights her lamp at night. Where does that energy come from?
options: burning coal at the power station
questions.explanation: The solar panel changes sunlight into electrical energy, which can be stored in a battery for the evening. Sunlight is a renewable source.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: A family burns 15 kg of firewood every week. If a biogas plant replaces all of it, they save ___ kg of wood in a year of 52 weeks.
questions.explanation: 15 × 52 = 780 kg. Biogas also means no smoke in the kitchen and fewer trees cut down.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Why is cooking with biogas healthier for a family than burning wood or dried dung?
questions.model_answer: Biogas burns with a clean flame and makes no smoke, so the family does not breathe smoke that harms their lungs.
questions.explanation: Smoke from wood and dung fills the kitchen and harms the lungs of women and children. Biogas burns cleanly and the leftover slurry makes fertiliser.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: In the simulation you choose the Sun, a solar panel and a light bulb. What is the energy chain?

sim.task: Open Energy Forms and Changes and choose the Systems screen. Choose the Sun as the energy source, the solar panel as the energy changer and the light bulb as the energy user. Watch the energy symbols.

questions.explanation: The solar panel changes the Sun's light into electrical energy. The bulb then changes the electricity back into light, with a little heat.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: In the simulation, the cyclist pedals to light a bulb through a generator. Put the energy changes in order.

sim.task: Open Energy Forms and Changes and choose the Systems screen. Choose the cyclist as the energy source, the generator as the changer and the light bulb as the user. Watch the energy symbols as the cyclist pedals.

sequence: chemical energy in the cyclist's body
kinetic energy of the pedalling cyclist
electrical energy from the generator
light from the bulb
questions.explanation: The cyclist's food energy (chemical) becomes movement (kinetic). The generator turns movement into electricity, and the bulb turns electricity into light.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: In the simulation, where does the skater have the most kinetic energy (movement energy)?

sim.task: Open Energy Skate Park Basics and choose the Intro screen. Switch on the energy bar graph. Release the skater from the top of the ramp and watch the bars as the skater rolls down.

options: at the bottom of the ramp
at the top, before letting go
at the same level on both sides
only when the skater is stopped
questions.explanation: As the skater rolls down, stored energy changes to kinetic energy. The kinetic energy is greatest at the bottom, where the skater moves fastest.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: Class 4A pulled a rubber band back by 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 cm. A toy car travelled 40, 85, 130, 170 and 210 cm. About how far would the car go for a pull of 12 cm?
questions.explanation: Each extra 2 cm of pull adds about 40 to 45 cm, so 12 cm gives about 210 + 40 = 250 cm. A more stretched band stores more energy, which becomes more kinetic energy.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: A bouncing ball rises a little lower after each bounce until it stops. Where does the ball's lost movement energy go?
options: It changes into heat and sound.
It is stored in the air as light.
questions.explanation: Energy is never destroyed, only changed. Each bounce turns some movement energy into heat and sound in the ball and the floor.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: 'Energy is never used up, it only changes form.' Use a bicycle that slows down and stops when you stop pedalling to explain this.
questions.model_answer: The bicycle's kinetic energy is not destroyed. Friction and air resistance change it into heat, and a little sound, in the tyres, brakes and air.
questions.explanation: When you stop pedalling, friction and air resistance slowly turn the kinetic energy into heat. The energy has changed form, not vanished.

questions.title: Energy and Work
questions.stem: An old bulb takes in 100 units of electrical energy (example numbers) and gives out only 10 units as light. The other ___ units are wasted, mostly as heat.
questions.explanation: 100 - 10 = 90 units are wasted as heat. An LED turns much more of its energy into light, so it wastes less and stays cool.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: All sounds are made by…
questions.explanation: A vibration is a very fast movement backwards and forwards. You can feel your voice box vibrate when you hum.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Match each instrument or voice to the part that vibrates.
questions.explanation: Hitting, plucking and blowing all make something vibrate. When you speak, your vocal cords vibrate.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Is the light or sound absorbed, reflected or refracted? Sort each example.
items: a black shirt gets hot in the sun
thick curtains make a room quieter
you see yourself in a mirror
you hear an echo in a big empty hall
a straw looks bent in a glass of water
a coin looks closer to the top of a bowl of water
questions.explanation: Dark, soft materials absorb. Shiny and hard surfaces reflect. Light bends (refracts) as it passes from water or glass into air.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Sound travels best through ___, because their particles are close together.
questions.explanation: In a solid the particles are packed close together, so they pass vibrations along very well. Sound travels well along a string or a wooden desk.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Sound can travel through empty space.
questions.explanation: Sound needs particles to pass the vibration on. There are no particles in empty space, so sound cannot travel there.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: A bigger vibration makes a ___ sound, and faster vibrations make a ___ pitch.
questions.explanation: Hit a drum harder and the vibrations are bigger, so it is louder. Faster vibrations give a higher pitch.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to show how you hear a dhol being played.
sequence: The drum skin is hit and vibrates.
The air next to the drum skin vibrates.
The vibration passes from particle to particle through the air.
The vibration reaches your ear.
questions.explanation: The vibration travels like a ripple, with each particle passing it to the next, until it reaches your ear.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Which surfaces are good at reflecting light? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Light-coloured and shiny surfaces reflect light well. Dark, dull surfaces absorb most of it, so they look dark.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Why do recording studios have soft foam on their walls?
questions.model_answer: Soft foam absorbs sound, so there are no echoes and noise from outside is muffled.
questions.explanation: Hard walls reflect sound and make echoes. Soft, thick materials absorb sound, so the recording is clear.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Anika wants a louder sound from her dhol. What should she do?
options: Stand much further away from the drum.
Hit the drum skin more gently.
Cover the drum skin with a thick cloth.
questions.explanation: A harder hit makes a bigger vibration, and a bigger vibration makes a louder sound. A cloth would muffle the sound.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Pitch tells us how loud a sound is.
questions.explanation: Pitch is how high or low a sound is. Loudness (volume) is how loud or soft it is, and is measured in decibels.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Hard, smooth surfaces such as walls and cliffs ___ sound, which can make an echo.
questions.explanation: An echo is sound that has been reflected back to you. Soft surfaces absorb sound instead, so they do not make echoes.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Which picture shows a **quiet**, **high** sound?
questions.image_alt: Four wave drawings A to D. A is loud and low, B is quiet and low, C is loud and high, D is quiet and high.
questions.explanation: Short waves mean a quiet sound and waves close together mean a high pitch. D has short, close waves.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Mina taps the bottles with a spoon. Which bottle vibrates the fastest?
questions.image_alt: Four bottles A to D. A has the least water and D has the most.
questions.explanation: Less water means less to shake, so bottle A vibrates fastest and gives the highest note. Fast vibrations mean a high pitch.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Use the scale. How many decibels louder is a plane taking off than people talking?
questions.image_alt: A loudness scale in decibels: leaves 20, birds 40, talking 60, busy traffic 80, loud music 100 and a plane taking off 120.
questions.explanation: The plane is at 120 dB and talking is at 60 dB, so the difference is 120 - 60 = 60 dB.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: The picture shows that a ray of light hits a mirror at the same angle as it bounces away.
questions.image_alt: A ray of light hitting a mirror and reflecting away. The angle in equals the angle out.
questions.explanation: The angle of the incoming ray equals the angle of the reflected ray. This is why a mirror gives a clear picture.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: In the picture, which instrument makes its sound when the air inside it vibrates?
questions.image_alt: A dhol (drum), an ektara (string instrument) and a banshi (flute).
questions.explanation: Blowing into the flute makes the column of air inside vibrate. The drum skin vibrates in the dhol, and the string vibrates in the ektara.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: The school hall in Chattogram has bare walls and a tiled floor, and every shout makes an echo. What would help most?
options: Paint the walls with shiny gloss paint.
Hang thick curtains and lay carpets.
Take all the furniture out of the hall.
Cover the floor with more tiles.
questions.explanation: Soft, thick materials absorb sound, so there is less to bounce back. Hard, shiny and empty spaces make echoes worse.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: On a sunny day in Chattogram, Nadia wears a black shirt and Priya wears a white shirt. Who feels hotter, and why?
options: Priya, because white colours absorb more light.
Both the same, because the Sun heats everyone equally.
Nadia, because black shirts reflect more light.
Nadia, because dark colours absorb more light.
questions.explanation: Dark objects absorb most of the light that hits them and warm up. White objects reflect much of it, so they stay cooler.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Joy puts a pencil in a glass of water. It looks broken, so she says the pencil really is broken. Is she right?
questions.explanation: Light bends (refracts) as it leaves the water and goes into the air, so the pencil only looks broken. The pencil itself is not damaged.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: During a storm in Sylhet, Sumi sees a flash of lightning and hears the thunder six seconds later. Why does she see it first?
options: Light travels much faster than sound.
Her eyes work faster than her ears.
The thunder is made later than the lightning.
questions.explanation: Light travels about 300 000 km every second, while sound in air travels only about 340 m a second. They start together, but the light arrives first.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: A family wants a quieter bedroom next to a noisy road. Which changes would help? Choose all that are right.
options: put a rug on the floor
fix egg boxes to one wall
cover the walls with a metal sheet
questions.explanation: Soft, thick and bumpy materials absorb sound. Hard, smooth surfaces such as metal reflect it instead.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: In the simulation, you move the frequency slider up. What happens to the sound?

sim.task: Open Sound Waves and choose the Single Source screen. Turn the sound on so that you can hear the speaker. Move the frequency slider from low to high and listen. Watch the waves.

questions.explanation: Frequency is how many vibrations happen each second. More vibrations each second give a higher pitch, and the waves are drawn closer together.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: In the simulation, when you move the amplitude slider up the waves look taller and the sound gets louder.

sim.task: Open Sound Waves and choose the Single Source screen. Turn the sound on and keep the frequency the same. Move the amplitude slider from low to high. Watch the waves and listen.

questions.explanation: Amplitude is the size of the vibration. A bigger vibration makes a louder sound, but the pitch does not change.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: In the simulation, the air is pumped out from around the speaker. What happens to the sound you hear?

sim.task: Open Sound Waves and choose the Air Pressure screen. Turn the sound on and listen. Then remove the air from around the speaker and listen again.

questions.explanation: With less air there are fewer particles to pass on the vibrations, so less sound reaches you. With no particles at all there would be silence.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: In the simulation, a white bulb with a red filter gives out only red light.

sim.task: Open Color Vision and choose the Single Bulb screen. Make the bulb give white light. Add the red filter and look at the colour of the light that comes out.

questions.explanation: A red filter lets red light through and absorbs the other colours. This is why light through a coloured filter takes on the colour of the filter.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Class 4D covered a box with a beeping phone using different materials and measured the loudness 1 m away: no cover 80 dB, newspaper 68 dB, foil 72 dB, bubble wrap 60 dB, cotton wool 52 dB. Which material muffled the sound most, and by how much?
questions.explanation: The lowest reading is the best muffler. Cotton wool gave 52 dB, which is 80 - 52 = 28 dB less than with no cover.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Astronauts on the Moon talk to each other by radio, even when they stand side by side. Explain why.
questions.model_answer: There is no air on the Moon, so there are no particles to carry sound vibrations. Radio signals can travel through empty space.
questions.explanation: Sound needs particles to pass the vibration on. On the Moon there is almost no air, but radio waves do not need particles.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Nadia sees lightning and hears thunder 3 seconds later. Sound in air travels about 340 m each second. About how far away is the storm?
questions.explanation: The light reaches her almost at once, so the 3 seconds is the sound travelling. 340 m × 3 = 1020 m, which is about 1 km.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Design an instrument from rubber bands stretched over a box. Explain how to make a high note and a low note.
questions.model_answer: Thin, tight, short rubber bands vibrate faster and give high notes. Thick, loose, long rubber bands vibrate more slowly and give low notes.
questions.explanation: Faster vibrations make a higher pitch and slower vibrations make a lower pitch. A thinner, tighter or shorter band vibrates faster.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Which question can a scientist answer by collecting evidence?
options: Does a bigger sail make a toy boat go faster?
Which colour of boat is the prettiest?
Is sailing more fun than swimming?
Do boats look nicest on a river?
questions.explanation: A testable question can be answered with measurements or observations. Questions about what is prettiest, nicest or most fun are opinions, so a test cannot settle them.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Match each measurement to the unit you would normally use.
pairs: the mass of a bag of rice
the time of a rickshaw ride
the volume of milk in a jug
questions.explanation: Choosing the right unit matters: mass is in grams or kilograms, force in newtons, time in seconds or minutes, volume in millilitres or litres, temperature in °C and loudness in decibels.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: In a fair test you change ___ thing, measure one thing and keep everything else the ___.
questions.explanation: If you change two things at once you cannot tell which one caused the result. The things you keep the same are called control variables.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Repeating a measurement and working out the mean makes your results more reliable.
questions.explanation: One measurement can contain a mistake. Repeating (often three times) and finding the mean gives results you can trust more, and it helps you spot an odd result.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Mina asks: "Does the amount of water change how tall bean seedlings grow?" Sort each item into its job in the investigation.
questions.explanation: Mina changes only the amount of water (independent variable) and measures the height (dependent variable). Everything else must stay the same so the test is fair.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: To find the mean of 8, 10 and 12, add them up and ___ the total by 3. The mean is ___.
questions.explanation: 8 + 10 + 12 = 30, and 30 ÷ 3 = 10. To find a mean, add the results and divide by how many results there are.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Choose the best graph for each set of results.
items: number of children who walk, cycle or take a bus to school
mass of a mango, a banana and a guava
water held by sand, soil and clay
height of a bean plant measured every day
temperature of a pot of water as it is heated each minute
length of a shadow measured every hour
questions.explanation: Use a bar chart when the thing you changed is in groups or words. Use a line graph when it is a number that changes smoothly, such as time.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Match each investigation to its type of enquiry.
pairs: Which kind of paper towel soaks up the most water?
Measuring a puppy's mass every week
Do taller children have longer feet?
Sorting shells into groups by shape
Using books to find out how the first aeroplane flew
questions.explanation: Scientists choose the type of enquiry that suits the question: a fair test changes one variable, while other enquiries watch change, look for patterns, sort things or use secondary sources.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Put the steps of a scientific investigation in order.
sequence: Ask a question that can be tested.
Make a prediction and give a reason.
Plan the test and decide what to keep the same.
Measure and record the results in a table.
Draw a graph and look for a pattern.
Write a conclusion and say how to improve.
questions.explanation: Good investigations follow a clear path: question, prediction, plan, results, pattern, and finally a conclusion with an evaluation.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Mina watches a bean seed germinate in a clear jar for a week. Which observations are the most useful? Choose all that are right.
options: On day 3 the seed coat splits and a root appears.
The shoot is 2 cm tall on day 5.
A lizard walked past the window.
The jar stands on the left of the shelf.
The root grows downwards and the shoot grows upwards.
questions.explanation: Useful observations describe the change you are studying, with numbers and times when possible. The lizard and the jar's position have nothing to do with germination.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: A model of the Solar System small enough to fit on a desk shows the real sizes and distances of the planets correctly.
questions.explanation: Models are useful but have limitations. To fit on a desk, the planets and their distances must be changed in scale, so the real Solar System is far bigger and emptier.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Which is the best heading for a column of times in a results table?
questions.explanation: A table heading says what was measured and gives the unit, such as Time (s). Then the numbers in the column do not need units.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Why did Jagadish Chandra Bose invent the crescograph?
options: To measure how loud plants are.
To magnify plant movements too small to see.
questions.explanation: Plant growth and movement are far too small and slow to see. The crescograph magnified them about 10 000 times, so Bose could collect new evidence and show that plants react to light, heat, touch and chemicals.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Raju wants to predict: "Will a puddle dry faster in the sun or in the shade?" Which is the best prediction?
options: It will dry faster in the shade because shade makes water lighter.
It will dry faster in the sun because heat makes water evaporate faster.
It will dry faster in the sun because I like sunny days.
It will dry at the same speed because all puddles are alike.
questions.explanation: A good prediction says what will happen and gives a reason from science. Warmer water evaporates faster. A liking for sunny days is not a scientific reason.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Read the thermometer scale with your eye level with the mark. What temperature does thermometer B show?
questions.image_alt: Three thermometers A, B and C with different liquid levels on a scale from 0 to 50 degrees Celsius.
questions.explanation: The liquid in thermometer B stops at 25 °C, halfway between the 20 and 30 marks. Always read the mark level with the top of the liquid.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Look at the three thermometers. The difference between the highest and the lowest reading is ___ °C.
questions.image_alt: Three thermometers A, B and C with different liquid levels on a scale from 0 to 50 degrees Celsius.
questions.explanation: The highest reading is thermometer C at 48 °C and the lowest is thermometer A at 12 °C. 48 − 12 = 36 °C.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Rafi hangs a bag from the forcemeter. What is the reading, with the correct unit?
questions.image_alt: A forcemeter with a spring, a pointer and a scale from 0 to 10.
questions.explanation: The pointer is at the 4 mark. Forces are measured in newtons (N), not grams, which are a unit of mass.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: The forcemeter shows ___ N. A second, lighter bag pulls with 4 N, so the first bag pulls ___ N more.
questions.image_alt: A forcemeter with a spring, a pointer and a scale from 0 to 10.
questions.explanation: The pointer is at 7 N. Comparing the bags: 7 − 4 = 3 N more.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Match each tool to what it measures.
questions.explanation: Each tool measures one thing: a balance measures mass, a stopwatch measures time, a thermometer measures temperature and a ruler measures length.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Priya wants to look closely at the tiny veins in a leaf. Which tool should she use?
questions.explanation: A magnifying glass (hand lens) makes small details look bigger, so it helps careful observation. The other tools measure time, length and mass.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Arif wants to know which of three fertilisers helps his chilli plants grow tallest. Which plan is the fairest?
options: Change the fertiliser and the pot size, so he sees which helps most.
Give each plant a fertiliser in the place that looks best.
Change only the fertiliser; give every plant the same soil, pot, water and light.
Use one fertiliser on all plants and change the amount of water.
questions.explanation: A fair test changes only one variable. If Arif changed the pot size or the place as well, he could not tell whether the fertiliser caused the difference.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Tuli wants to find which of four kinds of cloth dries fastest on the clothesline. Which things must she keep the same? Choose all that are right.
options: the amount of water in each cloth
where on the line each cloth hangs
questions.explanation: The type of cloth is what Tuli changes, and the time taken to dry is what she measures. Size, water and place are control variables, so they must stay the same.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Joy times a rickshaw crossing a bridge three times with a stopwatch: 62 s, 60 s and 64 s. The mean time is ___ s.
questions.explanation: 62 + 60 + 64 = 186, and 186 ÷ 3 = 62 s. Reporting the mean of three timings is more reliable than reporting one.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Lina feels hot and her mother thinks she has a fever. Which instrument and unit should they use?
questions.explanation: Body temperature is measured with a thermometer in degrees Celsius. The other instruments measure time, mass and volume.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Rafi's father plants a new kind of rice in one corner of his field and the old kind in the rest. The new rice gives more grain, so he says it is better. What is the biggest problem with his test?
options: He should have tested the rice in a laboratory.
He should have used a different fertiliser for each kind.
There is no problem: a bigger harvest always proves a better kind.
The two kinds grew in different places and were tested only once.
questions.explanation: The corner may have better soil or more water, so the place could explain the result. A fair test grows both kinds in the same conditions and repeats the test.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Sumi wants to find out which of three brands of soap washes a muddy cloth cleanest. Describe how she could make it a fair test.
questions.model_answer: Change only the brand of soap. Use cloths of the same size with the same amount of mud, the same amount of soap and water, and the same washing time. Repeat the test three times.
questions.explanation: A fair test changes one variable (the brand), measures one thing (how clean the cloth is) and keeps the cloth, mud, soap, water and time the same. Repeating makes the results more reliable.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Example class experiment: Class 5B dropped a ball from 1 m and measured the bounce height in five tries: 52 cm, 54 cm, 31 cm, 53 cm and 51 cm. In the third try the ball was dropped from a lower height by mistake. What is the best mean to report?
options: 52.5 cm, leaving out the 31 cm result
questions.explanation: The 31 cm result is an anomaly with a known cause, so it is left out. (52 + 54 + 53 + 51) ÷ 4 = 210 ÷ 4 = 52.5 cm. Using all five results gives 48.2 cm, which is pulled down by the mistake.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Example data: a cup of tea was left to cool. At 0, 5, 10 and 15 minutes its temperature was 80 °C, 62 °C, 50 °C and 43 °C. What is the best prediction for 20 minutes?
options: About 25 °C, because it falls by 18 °C every 5 minutes.
About 43 °C, because the tea has stopped cooling.
About 55 °C, because tea warms up again.
About 38 °C, because it keeps cooling but by smaller amounts each time.
questions.explanation: The drops are 18, 12 and 7 °C, so the tea cools more slowly as it gets closer to room temperature. The next drop is smaller still, about 5 °C, giving about 38 °C.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Example data: Imran tested three paper towels. Towel A has 2 layers and soaked up 10 ml of water. Towel B has 3 layers and soaked up 14 ml. Towel C has 4 layers and soaked up 18 ml. Which statements are supported by the data? Choose all that are right.
options: Towel C soaked up the most water.
Each extra layer soaked up about 4 ml more water.
Towels that cost more are always better.
Towel B soaked up less water than towel A.
The colour of the towel changed how much water it soaked up.
questions.explanation: A conclusion must be backed by the results. The table shows C took up the most and that each extra layer added about 4 ml. It says nothing about cost or colour, and B soaked up more than A, not less.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Anika predicted that salty water would freeze faster than tap water. Her results showed that the tap water froze first. She says: "My investigation failed because my prediction was wrong." Do you agree? Explain.
questions.model_answer: No, I disagree. A result that does not match the prediction is still useful evidence. Her investigation answered the question, and she can use the results to change her idea and make a new prediction.
questions.explanation: Science is about following the evidence. A surprising result teaches us something and can lead to a better explanation and a new prediction. (Salt really does lower the freezing point of water.)

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Organs that work together to do a big job make up an…
questions.explanation: An organ is a body part with a special job. Organs that work together form an organ system, such as the digestive system.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Match each organ to its job.
pairs: helps digestion and cleans the blood
a muscle that helps you breathe
questions.explanation: Each organ has a special job. The windpipe and the oesophagus are both tubes, but one carries air and the other carries food.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Sort each organ into its organ system.
questions.explanation: The digestive system breaks down food, the respiratory system handles breathing, the circulatory system moves blood, and the nervous system carries messages and controls the body.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Rafi touches a hot pan and quickly pulls his hand away. Put the path of the message in order.
sequence: Nerves in the skin of his hand sense the heat.
A message travels along nerves to the spinal cord and brain.
A message is sent back along nerves to the arm.
Muscles in his arm pull the hand away.
questions.explanation: The nervous system carries messages at high speed: in from the sense organ, to the spinal cord and brain, and out again to the muscles.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Food goes from the mouth down the ___ to the stomach. Most nutrients pass into the blood in the ___ intestine.
questions.explanation: The oesophagus (food pipe) carries food to the stomach. The windpipe carries air, and the large intestine mostly takes back water.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Oxygen is the waste gas that we breathe out.
questions.explanation: We breathe in oxygen, which passes into the blood. The waste gas that we breathe out is carbon dioxide.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Which jobs does the skeletal system do? Choose all that are right.
options: protects soft organs such as the brain
works with muscles so we can move
filters the blood to make urine
questions.explanation: Bones support and protect the body and work with muscles for movement. Pumping blood is the heart's job and filtering blood is the kidneys' job.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: What is your pulse?
options: the beat of blood pushed through an artery
the speed of nerve messages in the body
the number of breaths in each minute
the noise of food moving in your gut
questions.explanation: Each time the heart pumps, it pushes blood through the arteries, and you can feel this beat as your pulse, for example on your wrist.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Where is urine stored until you go to the toilet?
questions.explanation: The kidneys filter the blood and make urine. The urine is then stored in the bladder.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Match each organ system to its main job.
pairs: takes in oxygen and removes carbon dioxide
gets rid of waste made by the body
carries messages to control the body
questions.explanation: The six main organ systems each have their own job, and they work together to keep us alive.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Blood flows around the body in tubes called blood ___. The tiniest tubes are called ___.
questions.explanation: Blood vessels are arteries, veins and tiny capillaries. Capillaries reach every part of the body to deliver oxygen and nutrients.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: What does the diaphragm do?
options: It pumps blood to the lungs.
It is a muscle that helps you breathe.
It filters waste from the blood.
It carries air down to the lungs.
questions.explanation: The diaphragm is a sheet of muscle under the lungs that moves to help air go in and out. The heart pumps blood and the windpipe carries air.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Explain how oxygen gets from the air to the muscles in your legs.
questions.model_answer: You breathe air in through your nose and mouth, and it goes down the windpipe to the lungs. Oxygen passes into the blood in the lungs, and the heart pumps the blood around the body to the muscles.
questions.explanation: The respiratory system takes oxygen into the blood, and the circulatory system (heart and blood vessels) carries it to every cell. Both systems are needed.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: The nervous system is made of the brain only.
questions.explanation: The nervous system also includes the spinal cord and the nerves. The sense organs send information to it, and nerves carry messages around the body.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Match each number in the picture to the right bone.
questions.image_alt: A human skeleton with six bones numbered.
questions.explanation: The skull (1) protects the brain, the ribs (2) protect the heart and lungs, the spine (3) holds the body up and protects the spinal cord, and the thigh bone (5) is the longest bone in the body.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Match each organ or group of organs to the numbered part of the body where it is found.
questions.image_alt: An outline of a child with body parts numbered 1 to 11.
questions.explanation: The brain is in the head (1). The heart and lungs are in the chest (7), and the stomach and intestines are in the tummy (8).

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Which number shows a joint, where two bones meet?
questions.image_alt: An arm showing a bone, the biceps, the triceps and the elbow joint, numbered 1 to 4.
questions.explanation: Number 4 is the elbow joint, where the upper arm bone meets the lower arm bones. Numbers 2 and 3 are muscles.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: In the picture, the part numbered 4 protects the brain.
questions.image_alt: A human skeleton with six bones numbered.
questions.explanation: Number 4 is the pelvis, which supports the body and protects organs in the lower tummy. The skull (1) protects the brain.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Sort the pictures into the organ system each one belongs to.
questions.explanation: The brain controls the body and the eye is a sense organ that sends messages to it. The lungs are for breathing, the heart pumps blood, and teeth chew food at the start of digestion.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Which numbered part carries messages from the eye to the brain?
questions.image_alt: A cross-section of the eye with parts numbered 1 to 5.
questions.explanation: The optic nerve (5) is part of the nervous system. It carries messages from the retina (4) to the brain, which makes sense of what we see.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: At sports day Rima runs a race. Her heart beats much faster and she breathes hard. What is the best explanation?
options: Her bones need more blood to stop them breaking.
Her muscles need more oxygen, so breathing and heartbeat speed up.
Her stomach needs to digest her lunch faster.
Her kidneys need to make more urine quickly.
questions.explanation: Working muscles need more oxygen and energy. Faster breathing takes in more oxygen and a faster heartbeat carries it to the muscles more quickly.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: On a winter morning in Dhaka the air quality index (AQI) is 245, which is "very unhealthy" (201–300). What is the best decision for Moung's class?
options: Move sports indoors and wear masks outside.
Open all the windows for fresh air.
Run extra laps to make lungs stronger.
questions.explanation: Children breathe faster and deeper when they exercise, so they take in more polluted air. On very unhealthy days it is safer to stay indoors or limit time outside.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: After jogging, Imran counts 22 beats of his pulse in 15 seconds. His pulse rate is ___ beats per minute.
questions.explanation: There are four 15-second periods in one minute, so multiply by 4: 22 × 4 = 88 beats per minute.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Which actions help protect people's lungs in a polluted city? Choose all that are right.
options: wear a mask on very polluted days
spray water on dust at building sites
burn rubbish instead of collecting it
check that vehicles do not give out thick smoke
exercise next to a busy road at rush hour
questions.explanation: Masks, damping down dust and cleaner vehicles all reduce the tiny particles we breathe in. Burning rubbish and exercising beside heavy traffic add to the problem.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: A doctor puts a stethoscope on a child's chest to listen to the heart and lungs. Which two body systems is she checking?
questions.explanation: The heart belongs to the circulatory system and the lungs belong to the respiratory system. Both are found in the chest.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Nadia lives near a brick kiln in Dhaka and often coughs in winter. Explain how the smoke can harm her body.
questions.model_answer: Tiny particles in the smoke travel deep into her lungs and can cause coughing and lung infections. Some of the particles pass into the blood and can strain the heart, so the respiratory and circulatory systems are harmed.
questions.explanation: The smallest particles (PM2.5) are about 30 times thinner than a human hair. They reach deep into the lungs, and some even enter the blood, so they affect both breathing and the heart.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Example data: Tuli counted her pulse for 15 seconds. She counted 19 beats while resting and 31 beats after jogging. By how many beats per minute did her pulse rise?
questions.explanation: Resting: 19 × 4 = 76 beats per minute. After jogging: 31 × 4 = 124 beats per minute. The rise is 124 − 76 = 48. The answer 12 forgets to change 15 seconds into a minute.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: A person can live with only one kidney, but not without a heart. Which explanation is best?
options: Kidneys only store urine, so they are not needed.
One kidney can still filter enough blood, but nothing else can pump blood to the cells.
The heart is bigger, so it does more work than both kidneys.
Kidneys are smaller than the heart, so they matter less.
questions.explanation: One kidney can do the work of two. Without a heartbeat, oxygen and nutrients cannot reach the cells. Kidneys filter blood and make urine; the bladder stores it.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Example data: a school recorded the AQI each morning: Sat 120, Sun 158, Mon 205, Tue 310, Wed 175. The scale is: 101–150 unhealthy for sensitive groups, 151–200 unhealthy, 201–300 very unhealthy, 301 and above hazardous. Which statements are true? Choose all that are right.
options: The most polluted day was Tuesday, and the air was hazardous.
The air was "unhealthy" or worse on four of the five days.
Saturday's air was in the "very unhealthy" category.
Wednesday was more polluted than Monday.
questions.explanation: Tuesday (310) is the highest and is 301 or above. Sun, Mon, Tue and Wed are all 151 or more. Saturday (120) was only unhealthy for sensitive groups, and Wednesday (175) fell below Monday (205).

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Joy wrote four statements about the body. Which one is **not** correct?
options: Nutrients pass into the blood in the small intestine.
The heart pumps blood to the lungs, where it picks up oxygen.
The kidneys store urine until it leaves the body.
The ribs protect the heart and lungs.
questions.explanation: The kidneys filter the blood and make urine, but the bladder stores it. The other three statements are correct.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: Robert Hooke gave cells their name in 1665 after looking at a thin slice of…
questions.explanation: Hooke looked at cork through a microscope and saw rows of tiny boxes that reminded him of small rooms, so he called them cells.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: Match each specialised cell to its job.
pairs: gets shorter to move the body
stores energy and helps keep us warm
questions.explanation: Cells in the body are specialised: each kind has a shape that suits its job.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: Put the levels of organisation in order from smallest to largest.
sequence: cell
tissue
organ
organ system
organism
questions.explanation: Cells make tissues, tissues make organs, organs work together in organ systems, and all the organ systems together make a whole organism.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: A group of similar cells doing the same job is called a ___. Different tissues working together make an ___.
questions.explanation: Muscle tissue is a group of muscle cells. The heart is an organ because it is made of muscle tissue and other tissues working together.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: Most cells are too small to see without a microscope.
questions.explanation: Your body has about 30 trillion cells, and most of them are far too small for our eyes. We need a microscope to see them.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: A tissue is made of many different organs working together.
questions.explanation: A tissue is made of many similar cells doing the same job. It is an organ that is made of different tissues.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: Sort each example into its level of organisation.
items: muscle tissue in the heart wall
questions.explanation: A cell is the smallest unit, similar cells form a tissue, tissues form an organ such as the brain, and organs working together form an organ system.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: Which parts do animal cells have? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Animal cells have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus. The cell wall and chloroplasts are extra parts found in plant cells.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: Red blood cells are round and dented in the middle. How does this shape help them?
options: It lets them get shorter to move the body.
It gives a large surface for carrying oxygen.
It lets them store fat for energy.
It lets them send messages along nerves.
questions.explanation: The dented disc shape gives a large surface for carrying oxygen, and the cells can bend to squeeze through tiny blood vessels.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: Match each cell shape to the job it helps the cell to do.
pairs: carries messages quickly over long distances
long and able to get shorter
flat and fitting together like tiles
carries oxygen and squeezes through tiny vessels
questions.explanation: In specialised cells the shape fits the job. Long branching nerve cells reach far; tile-like skin cells leave no gaps for germs.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: Which part of an animal cell is a thin skin that controls what goes in and out?
questions.explanation: The cell membrane holds the cell together and controls what passes in and out. The nucleus is the control centre and the cytoplasm is the jelly where the work happens.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: An animal cell has three main parts: the cell ___, the jelly-like ___ and the ___, which is the control centre.
questions.explanation: The membrane is the thin skin, the cytoplasm is the jelly where the cell's work happens, and the nucleus holds the instructions for the cell.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: Explain how the shape of a nerve cell helps it do its job.
questions.model_answer: A nerve cell is long and thin with branches, so it can carry messages quickly over a long distance and connect to many other cells.
questions.explanation: The long, branching shape lets nerve cells carry messages around the body at high speed and pass them on to other cells.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek saw living cells, such as blood cells, that Hooke had not seen. Why was he able to?
options: He used a bigger piece of cork.
He could see cells with his eyes alone.
questions.explanation: Leeuwenhoek made better lenses, so he could see much smaller things. A better instrument gave him new evidence, including living cells and tiny creatures in pond water.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: Match each number in the picture to the name of the part.
questions.image_alt: An animal cell with three parts numbered 1 to 3.
questions.explanation: The cell membrane (1) is the outer skin, the cytoplasm (2) is the jelly inside and the nucleus (3) is the control centre.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: In the picture, the part numbered 1 is the jelly where the cell's work happens.
questions.image_alt: An animal cell with three parts numbered 1 to 3.
questions.explanation: Part 1 is the cell membrane, the thin skin around the cell. The jelly where the work happens is the cytoplasm, part 2.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: A plant cell has all the parts of this animal cell and also a tough cell wall. Where would the cell wall be?
questions.image_alt: An animal cell with three parts numbered 1 to 3.
questions.explanation: The cell wall is a strong layer around the outside of a plant cell, just beyond the cell membrane (1). It helps the plant stand up without bones.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: Which two numbered parts of the arm are mostly made of muscle tissue? Choose all that are right.
questions.image_alt: An arm showing a bone (1), the biceps (2), the triceps (3) and the elbow joint (4).
questions.explanation: The biceps (2) and triceps (3) are muscles, so they are made of muscle tissue, which is full of muscle cells that can get shorter. Number 1 is a bone and number 4 is a joint.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: Is each picture a whole organism or only an organ? Sort the pictures.
questions.explanation: An organ is one part of a body with a special job. An organism is a whole living thing, such as a cat, a fish or a rice plant.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: All living things are made of cells. Which of these is made of cells?
questions.explanation: A rice plant is a living thing, so it is made of cells. Rocks, coins and plastic bottles were never alive and are not made of cells.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
